news.content_title: Gilead Expands Access to Investigational Obeldesivir for Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Through Voluntary Licensing
news.content: FOSTER CITY, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 16, 2026-- Gilead Sciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: GILD) today announced that it has signed royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). The agreements cover 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, consistent with the geographic scope of Gilead’s existing voluntary licensing agreements for remdesivir for COVID-19 and include all African countries that have reported cases during the current Ebola BVD outbreak. The agreements are intended to support manufacturing readiness, technology transfer and supply planning while the ongoing Ebola Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (EBO-PEP) field trial evaluates obeldesivir as PEP for Ebola BVD. Key Highlights Royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers cover primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries and are intended to support potential future access to investigational obeldesivir. EBO-PEP is a Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled trial being coordinated by ALIMA and partners evaluating investigational obeldesivir as PEP for individuals at high risk of developing Ebola BVD. Gilead is updating its existing voluntary licensing agreements for remdesivir to include filovirus disease, supporting potential future access should results from the ongoing World Health Organization (WHO)-sponsored PARTNERS trial support its use as a treatment for Ebola BVD and pending potential regulatory approvals. Gilead recently donated more than 2,000 vials of remdesivir to Kenya for investigational use as treatment and PEP for people with confirmed Ebola BVD or individuals with a close contact exposure. “Responding to emerging infectious diseases, including Ebola virus disease, requires not only scientific innovation, but also early planning and collaboration to help ensure that effective medicines can reach the people who need them as quickly as possible,” said Jaime McCoy, Vice President, Gilead Patient Solutions, Gilead Sciences. “These agreements reflect our commitment to preparing for future access while clinical research is ongoing, so that we are better positioned to respond if these investigational medicines demonstrate benefit and gain regulatory approval.” The manufacturers that have entered into voluntary licensing agreements with Gilead are Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories. Technology transfer discussions are already underway, and agreements with additional manufacturers are under discussion. Under the agreements, the companies will be authorized to manufacture and supply obeldesivir in the licensed territory if supported by clinical data and applicable regulatory authorizations. Obeldesivir has demonstrated preclinical activity across multiple filoviruses but is not approved for the PEP of filovirus disease in any country. These agreements are part of Gilead's broader approach to outbreak preparedness, which includes clinical research, manufacturing and supply planning, technology transfer, and collaboration with governments, public health agencies and global health partners. As part of its response to the current Ebola BVD outbreak, Gilead has provided compassionate use donations of remdesivir to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and Kenya totaling more than 38,000 vials. About Obeldesivir Obeldesivir is an investigational antiviral that has been evaluated in clinical trials for COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and has demonstrated preclinical activity across multiple filoviruses. It is currently being evaluated in the Ebola Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (EBO-PEP) trial, a partner-led Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled field trial evaluating the efficacy of obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for individuals at high risk of developing Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). Obeldesivir is not approved for the PEP of filovirus disease or for any indication in any country. About Remdesivir Remdesivir is a nucleotide analog prodrug invented and developed by Gilead, building on more than a decade of the company’s antiviral research. Remdesivir has broad-spectrum antiviral activity both in vitro and in animal models against multiple viral pathogens, including Marburg, Ebola, SARS, MERS and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. Remdesivir has been approved as a COVID-19 treatment in approximately 50 countries worldwide. To date, remdesivir has been made available to more than 14.5 million patients around the world, including more than 8.1 million people in middle- and low-income countries through Gilead’s voluntary licensing program. The clinical efficacy of remdesivir for the treatment of Ebola BVD has not been established. Remdesivir is currently not approved in any country for the treatment or prevention of Ebola BVD. For more information about Gilead’s commitment to global health, visit Gilead.com . About Gilead Sciences Gilead Sciences, Inc. is a biopharmaceutical company that has pursued and achieved breakthroughs in medicine for more than three decades, with the goal of creating a healthier world for all people. The company is committed to advancing innovative medicines to prevent and treat life-threatening diseases, including HIV, viral hepatitis, COVID-19, cancer and inflammation. In 2025, Gilead announced a $32 billion investment to further strengthen its U.S. footprint to power the next era of discovery, job creation and public health preparedness – while continuing to invest globally to ensure patients everywhere benefit from its scientific innovation. Gilead operates in more than 35 countries worldwide, with headquarters in Foster City, Calif. Forward-Looking Statements This press release includes forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 that are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors, including Gilead’s ability to initiate, progress or complete clinical trials within currently anticipated timelines or at all, and the possibility of unfavorable results from ongoing or additional clinical trials, including those involving obeldesivir and remdesivir (such as the partner-led EBO-PEP and PARTNERS trials); uncertainties relating to regulatory applications and related filing and approval timelines, including additional pending and potential applications for obeldesivir and remdesivir; the risk that any regulatory approvals, if granted, may be subject to significant limitations on use or subject to withdrawal or other adverse actions by the applicable regulatory authority; the possibility that Gilead may make a strategic decision to discontinue development of obeldesivir and remdesivir for indications currently under evaluation; Gilead’s ability to effectively manage, execute and realize the anticipated benefits from the access strategy relating to obeldesivir and remdesivir, including voluntary licensing arrangements and external partnerships relating to obeldesivir and remdesivir; difficulties or unanticipated expenses in connection with such access strategy, licensing arrangements and partnerships; and any assumptions underlying any of the foregoing. news.content_original: FOSTER CITY, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 16, 2026-- Gilead Sciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: GILD) today announced that it has signed royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). The agreements cover 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, consistent with the geographic scope of Gilead’s existing voluntary licensing agreements for remdesivir for COVID-19 and include all African countries that have reported cases during the current Ebola BVD outbreak. The agreements are intended to support manufacturing readiness, technology transfer and supply planning while the ongoing Ebola Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (EBO-PEP) field trial evaluates obeldesivir as PEP for Ebola BVD. Key Highlights Royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers cover primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries and are intended to support potential future access to investigational obeldesivir. EBO-PEP is a Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled trial being coordinated by ALIMA and partners evaluating investigational obeldesivir as PEP for individuals at high risk of developing Ebola BVD. Gilead is updating its existing voluntary licensing agreements for remdesivir to include filovirus disease, supporting potential future access should results from the ongoing World Health Organization (WHO)-sponsored PARTNERS trial support its use as a treatment for Ebola BVD and pending potential regulatory approvals. Gilead recently donated more than 2,000 vials of remdesivir to Kenya for investigational use as treatment and PEP for people with confirmed Ebola BVD or individuals with a close contact exposure. “Responding to emerging infectious diseases, including Ebola virus disease, requires not only scientific innovation, but also early planning and collaboration to help ensure that effective medicines can reach the people who need them as quickly as possible,” said Jaime McCoy, Vice President, Gilead Patient Solutions, Gilead Sciences. “These agreements reflect our commitment to preparing for future access while clinical research is ongoing, so that we are better positioned to respond if these investigational medicines demonstrate benefit and gain regulatory approval.” The manufacturers that have entered into voluntary licensing agreements with Gilead are Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories. Technology transfer discussions are already underway, and agreements with additional manufacturers are under discussion. Under the agreements, the companies will be authorized to manufacture and supply obeldesivir in the licensed territory if supported by clinical data and applicable regulatory authorizations. Obeldesivir has demonstrated preclinical activity across multiple filoviruses but is not approved for the PEP of filovirus disease in any country. These agreements are part of Gilead's broader approach to outbreak preparedness, which includes clinical research, manufacturing and supply planning, technology transfer, and collaboration with governments, public health agencies and global health partners. As part of its response to the current Ebola BVD outbreak, Gilead has provided compassionate use donations of remdesivir to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and Kenya totaling more than 38,000 vials. About Obeldesivir Obeldesivir is an investigational antiviral that has been evaluated in clinical trials for COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and has demonstrated preclinical activity across multiple filoviruses. It is currently being evaluated in the Ebola Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (EBO-PEP) trial, a partner-led Phase 3 randomized, placebo-controlled field trial evaluating the efficacy of obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for individuals at high risk of developing Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). Obeldesivir is not approved for the PEP of filovirus disease or for any indication in any country. About Remdesivir Remdesivir is a nucleotide analog prodrug invented and developed by Gilead, building on more than a decade of the company’s antiviral research. Remdesivir has broad-spectrum antiviral activity both in vitro and in animal models against multiple viral pathogens, including Marburg, Ebola, SARS, MERS and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. Remdesivir has been approved as a COVID-19 treatment in approximately 50 countries worldwide. To date, remdesivir has been made available to more than 14.5 million patients around the world, including more than 8.1 million people in middle- and low-income countries through Gilead’s voluntary licensing program. The clinical efficacy of remdesivir for the treatment of Ebola BVD has not been established. Remdesivir is currently not approved in any country for the treatment or prevention of Ebola BVD. For more information about Gilead’s commitment to global health, visit Gilead.com . About Gilead Sciences Gilead Sciences, Inc. is a biopharmaceutical company that has pursued and achieved breakthroughs in medicine for more than three decades, with the goal of creating a healthier world for all people. The company is committed to advancing innovative medicines to prevent and treat life-threatening diseases, including HIV, viral hepatitis, COVID-19, cancer and inflammation. In 2025, Gilead announced a $32 billion investment to further strengthen its U.S. footprint to power the next era of discovery, job creation and public health preparedness – while continuing to invest globally to ensure patients everywhere benefit from its scientific innovation. Gilead operates in more than 35 countries worldwide, with headquarters in Foster City, Calif. Forward-Looking Statements This press release includes forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 that are subject to risks, uncertainties and other factors, including Gilead’s ability to initiate, progress or complete clinical trials within currently anticipated timelines or at all, and the possibility of unfavorable results from ongoing or additional clinical trials, including those involving obeldesivir and remdesivir (such as the partner-led EBO-PEP and PARTNERS trials); uncertainties relating to regulatory applications and related filing and approval timelines, including additional pending and potential applications for obeldesivir and remdesivir; the risk that any regulatory approvals, if granted, may be subject to significant limitations on use or subject to withdrawal or other adverse actions by the applicable regulatory authority; the possibility that Gilead may make a strategic decision to discontinue development of obeldesivir and remdesivir for indications currently under evaluation; Gilead’s ability to effectively manage, execute and realize the anticipated benefits from the access strategy relating to obeldesivir and remdesivir, including voluntary licensing arrangements and external partnerships relating to obeldesivir and remdesivir; difficulties or unanticipated expenses in connection with such access strategy, licensing arrangements and partnerships; and any assumptions underlying any of the foregoing. These and other risks, uncertainties and factors are described in detail in Gilead’s Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, as filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. news.content_zh: 吉利德科学公司通过与三个仿制药制造商签订免版税自愿许可协议,扩大了其在研 抗病毒药物 奥贝昔韦的使用范围,未来可能用作埃博拉本迪布焦病毒病 (BVD) 的暴露后预防 (PEP)。这些协议主要覆盖 127 个低收入和中低收入国家,包括所有报告 BVD 病例的非洲国家。该计划是吉利德为 暴发 场景做准备、支持制造准备、技术转让和供应规划的更广泛战略的一部分。由 ALIMA 和合作伙伴协调进行的 EBO-PEP 现场试验正在评估奥贝昔韦作为 PEP 对 BVD 高风险个体的疗效。然而,奥贝昔韦目前尚未在任何国家被批准用于丝状病毒病的 PEP,其对 BVD 的临床疗效仍未得到证实。吉利德还向肯尼亚、刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 和乌干达捐赠了瑞德西韦,用于治疗 BVD 确诊病例的研究用途。这些协议反映了吉利德的承诺,即确保有效的药物到达有需要的人手中,等待监管部门的批准和临床数据。

news.content_title: Tedros: 'Six months ago, I declared the Bundibugyo virus Ebola outbreak in the DRC a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. Since then, over 11,000 cases and 5400 deaths have been recorded across eight provinces, making this the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history, with children bearing a heavy burden. Yet amid immense hardship, local responders and global partners, under the leadership of the government, are driving hard-won progress. Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly. My deepest gratitude goes to the Congolese nurses, doctors, community health workers, contact tracers, and burial teams working under extraordinary pressure. Because of your courage, around 3000 people have recovered and returned home.'

analysis.brief_en: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus declared the Bundibugyo virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May 2026. As of 15 November 2026, the outbreak has resulted in over 11,000 cases and 5400 deaths across eight provinces, making it the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC's history. Children have been disproportionately affected. Despite the challenges, local responders and global partners are making progress, with transmission slowing in several early epicentres and clinical trials advancing rapidly. The overall risk remains very high in the DRC and high in neighboring countries, but regional and global levels have lower risk due to preparedness and rapid detection measures. Tedros expressed gratitude for the efforts of Congolese healthcare workers and highlighted the importance of continued collaboration in the response.

news.source_body_en: WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus declared the Bundibugyo virus Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 17 May 2026. As of 15 November 2026, the outbreak has resulted in over 11,000 cases and 5400 deaths across eight provinces, making it the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak in the DRC's history. Children have been disproportionately affected. Despite the challenges, local responders and global partners are making progress, with transmission slowing in several early epicentres and clinical trials advancing rapidly. The overall risk remains very high in the DRC and high in neighboring countries, but regional and global levels have lower risk due to preparedness and rapid detection measures. Tedros expressed gratitude for the efforts of Congolese healthcare workers and highlighted the importance of continued collaboration in the response.
news.content_zh: 世卫组织总干事谭德塞于 2026 年 5 月 17 日宣布刚果民主共和国(DRC)的本迪布焦病毒埃博拉病毒 暴发 为国际关注的突发公共卫生事件(PHEIC)。截至 2026 年 11 月 15 日,暴发 已在八个省份造成超过 11,000 例病例和 5400 人死亡,使其成为国际关注的突发公共卫生事件。刚果民主共和国历史上规模最大、最致命的埃博拉病毒 暴发。儿童受到的影响尤为严重。尽管面临挑战,当地应对人员和全球合作伙伴仍在取得进展,传播 在几个早期震中的进展放缓,临床试验进展迅速。刚果民主共和国的总体风险仍然很高,邻国也很高,但由于做好准备和快速检测措施,区域和全球层面的风险较低。谭德塞对刚果医护人员的努力表示感谢,并强调在应对工作中继续合作的重要性。

news.content: News Around the World Mobility data predicted spread of Bundibugyo virus in DR Congo — News-Medical UA.NEWS 17 November 2026 02:43 Scientists from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and international partners found that human movement, rather than geography or population size, was the key factor in the rapid initial spread of Bundibugyo virus disease in Ituri and neighboring provinces. This was reported by News-Medical , citing a study published in the journal Science. The first weeks of the outbreak Researchers combined detailed data on disease cases and testing with anonymized mobile phone data on population movements. According to their estimates, from early May to June 1, 2026, the number of cases doubled approximately every 10 days. The outbreak was declared on May 15, 2026. Over three weeks, the number of health zones with confirmed cases increased by 12, while the number of health areas increased by 49. More than 50 scientists from over 25 institutions took part in the work, including the DR Congo National Institute of Biomedical Research, the University of Kinshasa, Africa CDC, WHO, the University of Oxford, and the Pasteur Institute. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Predicting the spread The team analyzed anonymized movement flows from Mongbwalu, Bunia, and Rwampara. A model based on these data predicted almost flawlessly which health zones would record cases of the disease and outperformed models relying solely on population size. The study authors noted that mobility and travel-time data available in the first days after an outbreak is reported can help pre-position surveillance, diagnostic, and medical care resources in areas to which the infection may spread next. analysis.brief_en: Uganda's border communities are taking proactive measures to defend against the threat of Ebola Virus Disease, according to a UNICEF press release published on 12 November 2026. The report emphasizes the role of UNICEF in supporting efforts to protect children's health and rights in the region. However, the evidence does not provide specific details about the number of cases, deaths, or exposures related to the disease. The focus is on community-based initiatives and the broader context of UNICEF's work in conflict and disease outbreaks. The report does not mention any confirmed or suspected outbreaks, but it underscores the importance of preparedness and prevention in mitigating the risk of Ebola Virus Disease. The information is based on a press release and does not include detailed data on the scale of the impact or the current status of the disease in Uganda.

Facebook Twitter Print Email World News in Brief: Ebola cases double in DR Congo, chemical exposure starts before birth, Türk concern over EU-Rwanda transfer plan 17 November 2026 Health The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has more than doubled in three months, with more than 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths now reported in 67 health zones across eight provinces, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday. Tweet URL Opening the third meeting of WHO’s Emergency Committee on the Bundibugyo virus disease epidemic, Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said children were “paying a terrible price”. They account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths, and seven in ten children under five with confirmed Ebola have died. “The risk beyond the DRC’s borders is not theoretical,” he said. Kenya has reported nine cases linked to an imported case, including two deaths, and Nigeria has reported one imported case. He also expressed concern that some countries continue to apply blanket travel restrictions, which hinder the response and discourage countries from reporting outbreaks quickly. Progress made Elaborating on the progress made, Dr Tedros said rapid transmission has been halted in most of the early epicentres, and the number of laboratories able to test for the virus has risen from two to more than two dozen. Two candidate vaccines developed specifically for Bundibugyo virus will be added to an ongoing vaccine trial in the coming weeks. “But progress in some places is not control of the outbreak as a whole,” Dr. Tedros warned. Between 400 and 500 new cases are still reported every week, and two-thirds of confirmed deaths occur outside Ebola treatment centres, a sign that infections are being identified too late. Exposure to hormone-disrupting chemicals can begin before birth Exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) can begin before birth, with a broader range of effects on human and environmental health than previously understood, a new report released by the UN Enviornment Programme (UNEP) and WHO revealed on Tuesday. The chemicals, which can interfere with the body’s hormones, have been detected in blood, breast milk and cord blood. Early exposure can have lasting effects on brain development, growth and reproductive health. Tweet URL The State of the Science on Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals 2026 is the first major global update since 2012. It finds stronger evidence linking EDCs to effects on fertility, brain development, thyroid and other hormone regulation, metabolism, immunity and cardiovascular health. In fish, birds, amphibians and mammals, exposure has been linked to impaired reproduction, development and behaviour. ‘Long-lasting’ impact “These effects can be long-lasting and, in some cases, irreversible,” said Sheila Aggarwal Khan, Director of UNEP’s Industry and Economy Division. More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures are registered for production and use globally, yet only a small fraction have been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties. According to the study, the global cost of diseases associated with EDC exposure could amount to one per cent or more of global GDP. “Protecting health means preventing harmful exposures before they occur,” said Bruce Gordon, acting Director of WHO’s Department of Environment, Climate Change, One Health and Migration. The report was launched at the first International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals, which runs in Geneva until 20 November. Türk raises rights concerns over EU-Rwanda transfer proposal UN human rights chief Volker Türk has raised concern about the human rights risks of a proposal to transfer people from five European Union countries to Rwanda, “where they have no genuine connection and which has its own set of human rights challenges”. Mr. Türk said his Office was not privy to the text of the proposal. “The solution does not lie in single measures – often very costly – of finding countries far away to deal with one aspect of migration governance, or in externalising human rights obligations,” he said. Instead, he called for the drivers of migration to be tackled head-on, including through investment that creates viable opportunities at home. Those drivers include human rights challenges, huge inequalities, an inequitable economic and financial system that disadvantages many countries in the Global South, a surge in violent conflicts and heightened geopolitical tensions. At the same time, societies in the Global North are rapidly ageing and grappling with labour shortages, Mr. Türk noted. He called for a comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights, including expanded regular migration pathways. health Migrants and refugees Facebook Twitter Print Email Back to top

analysis.time: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has more than doubled in three months, with more than 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths now reported as of 17 November 2026 (N2). Between 400 and 500 new cases are still reported every week (N11).
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically in 67 health zones across eight provinces (N2). Children are highlighted as a vulnerable population, with more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths involving children (N4).
analysis.event: The WHO Director-General, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, reported that the Ebola outbreak in the DRC has more than doubled in three months, with over 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths (N2). He also noted that two-thirds of confirmed deaths occur outside Ebola treatment centres, indicating late identification of infections (N11).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has resulted in over 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths in the DRC (N2). Among children, seven in ten under five with confirmed Ebola have died (N4). The WHO head emphasized that the risk beyond the DRC’s borders is not theoretical (N5).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Progress has been made in halting rapid transmission in most early epicentres and increasing the number of laboratories able to test for the virus from two to more than two dozen (N8). Two candidate vaccines for the Bundibugyo virus will be added to an ongoing trial (N9). However, the outbreak is not fully controlled, and the risk remains significant (N10).

analysis.brief_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has more than doubled in three months, with over 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths reported as of 17 November 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Children are particularly affected, accounting for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths, with seven in ten children under five with confirmed Ebola dying. The WHO head warned that the risk of the outbreak spreading beyond the DRC is not theoretical. Despite progress, including the halting of rapid transmission in most early epicentres and an increase in testing laboratories, the outbreak remains uncontrolled. Two candidate vaccines for the Bundibugyo virus will be added to an ongoing trial. The report also highlights the broader implications of chemical exposure starting before birth, with potential long-term effects on health. Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk expressed concerns over a proposal to transfer migrants from EU countries to Rwanda, citing human rights risks and the need for a comprehensive approach to migration governance.

news.source_body_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has more than doubled in three months, with over 11,000 cases and 5,400 deaths reported as of 17 November 2026, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Children are particularly affected, accounting for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths, with seven in ten children under five with confirmed Ebola dying. The WHO head warned that the risk of the outbreak spreading beyond the DRC is not theoretical. Despite progress, including the halting of rapid transmission in most early epicentres and an increase in testing laboratories, the outbreak remains uncontrolled. Two candidate vaccines for the Bundibugyo virus will be added to an ongoing trial. The report also highlights the broader implications of chemical exposure starting before birth, with potential long-term effects on health. Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker Türk expressed concerns over a proposal to transfer migrants from EU countries to Rwanda, citing human rights risks and the need for a comprehensive approach to migration governance.
news.content_zh: 根据世界卫生组织 (WHO) 的数据,截至 2026 年 11 月 17 日,刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 的埃博拉病毒 暴发 在三个月内增加了一倍多,报告病例数超过 11,000 例,死亡人数 5,400 人。儿童受到的影响尤其严重,占确诊病例的四分之一以上和死亡人数的三分之一,其中十分之七的五岁以下儿童确诊感染埃博拉病毒而死亡。世卫组织负责人警告说,暴发 传播到刚果民主共和国以外地区的风险并非理论上存在。尽管取得了一些进展,包括在大多数早期震中停止了快速 传播 以及增加了测试实验室,但 暴发 仍然不受控制。Bundibugyo 病毒的两个候选 疫苗 将被添加到正在进行的试验中。该报告还强调了出生前开始接触化学物质的更广泛影响,对健康可能产生长期影响。与此同时,联合国人权事务高级专员沃尔克·蒂尔克对将移民从欧盟国家转移到卢旺达的提议表示担忧,理由是存在人权风险以及需要采取全面的移民治理方法。

news.content_title: Ebola outbreak defies control as war and hunger fuel crisis six months in
news.content: Subscribe Digital Print November 18, 2026 Subscribe Digital Print Cyberattacks APEC Foreign community in Japan Latest News Today's print edition Home Delivery JAPAN Politics Society Crime & Legal Science & Health Explainer History WORLD Politics Crime & Legal Science & Health Society ASIA PACIFIC Politics Crime & Legal Science & Health Society BUSINESS Companies Economy Markets Tech SPORTS Sumo Soccer Baseball Basketball Tennis Olympics More sports OPINION Editorials Commentary Geoeconomic Briefing Environment CLIMATE CHANGE Energy SUSTAINABILITY WILDLIFE EARTH SCIENCE LIFE Travel Digital Food & Drink Style & Design Language Lifestyle CULTURE Film Books Music Art TV & Streaming Stage Entertainment news COMMUNITY Voices Issues How-tos Our Lives My Account My Bookmarks Logout Subscribe for more access WORLD / Science & Health Ebola outbreak defies control as war and hunger fuel crisis six months in People pass through at an Ebola health checkpoint on the outskirts of Biakato, Congo, a small town deep in the rainforest which now accounts for as many as one-quarter of the sprawling country’s new Ebola cases, on Oct. 19. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times BLOOMBERG SHARE/SAVE X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link Nov 16, 2026 Listen to this article 7 min Six months into the biggest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s history, containing the virus increasingly depends on solving problems far beyond Ebola — hunger, armed conflict, mistrust and a health system already buckling under the strain. More than 11,000 people have been infected and 5,500 have died since the outbreak was declared May 15. For months, Ebola has been killing roughly 240 people a week, the equivalent of about one and a half Boeing Co. 737 passenger jets crashing every week. “It’s a systems problem compounded by basically geography, insecurity, conflict, poor roads, mistrust,” said William Clemmer, a physician who has worked in Congo for three decades and is senior regional health adviser for Corus International based in Goma. Clemmer, 69, who has worked on four Ebola outbreaks, said many health facilities entered the current crisis without reliable water, electricity, sterilization, waste disposal or supply systems. Delivering protective equipment can only accomplish so much if clinics lack the basic infrastructure needed to use it safely, he said. Congo’s own data illustrate the problem. As of Nov. 14, the country had recorded 11,376 confirmed infections and 5,568 deaths, for a fatality rate of almost 49%. The outbreak had reached 68 health zones across eight provinces. In North Kivu province, 153 Ebola patients and suspected cases were being cared for in ordinary health facilities outside designated treatment and isolation centers on Nov. 14. People who aren’t identified and isolated can continue spreading Ebola at home, in clinics and during funerals. A local shop keeper is helped at a makeshift treatment center for Ebola patients in Biakato, Congo, on Oct. 16. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times About two-thirds of Ebola deaths have recently occurred in communities rather than treatment centers, according to Medecins Sans Frontieres. “When two-thirds of our deaths occur in local communities, that basically tells us that either people are being detected too late or they’re not reaching care at all,” Clemmer said. “That is an indication not just of failure of surveillance, but also of access, trust and security.” Fear factor The International Rescue Committee said its teams recently documented 84 rumors, including a recurring belief that people taken to Ebola treatment centers “do not return home alive.” The group said fear is discouraging some women from seeking routine medical care, including postnatal services. The outbreak’s roughly 50% fatality rate makes that reluctance understandable, Clemmer said. Unlike the 2018-2020 Ebola epidemic in eastern Congo, responders don’t yet have a vaccine or treatment proven to work against the Bundibugyo strain driving the current outbreak. Telling families that a relative needs to enter a treatment center where many patients are dying can fuel resistance, he said. The consequences extend far beyond Ebola. Almost 29 million people in Congo already face acute food insecurity, a number projected to exceed 30 million in the first half of next year, according to United Nations agencies. More than 11 million of them are in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu, the eastern provinces at the center of the country’s humanitarian crisis. Conflict displaces families from their farms and livelihoods, while Ebola restrictions and fear can further disrupt farming and trade. For health officials, that creates another obstacle: asking someone exposed to Ebola to isolate is harder when leaving home may be necessary to earn money or find food. “These people have the responsibility of working, of getting food for their family,” Clemmer said. Violence poses a more direct threat, with armed groups killing more people than Ebola itself in some affected areas, Julien Harneis, the U.N.’s senior Ebola response coordinator, said last week. Health care workers carry the corpse of a victim from a makeshift Ebola treatment center in Biakato, Congo on Oct. 18. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times Over one recent weekend, more people were murdered by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) than died from the virus, he said in a post marking six months since the outbreak was declared. The violence is also making the epidemic harder to stop. Harneis said one of the response’s most pressing challenges is finding ways to improve contact tracing in conflict areas where attacks by the ADF and other armed groups are impeding the work. He also called for greater engagement with private health providers, where he said most people initially seek care. Scientific hope There are reasons for optimism. Transmission has declined in some former hotspots, neighboring countries have so far avoided sustained spread, and clinical trials under way in Congo could eventually provide vaccines and treatments specifically suited to Bundibugyo Ebola. Thousands of people are already receiving Merck & Co.’s Ervebo vaccine while scientists investigate whether the shot, approved against Zaire ebolavirus, can also protect against Bundibugyo. Africa CDC said emerging evidence suggests it may provide some cross-protection and supports its use in high-risk children while the evaluation continues. Meanwhile, two vaccines designed specifically against Bundibugyo — one developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and another from Moderna — are set to enter a late-stage trial in Congo. Researchers will test whether they can protect people exposed to the virus from developing severe disease or dying, with results expected in early 2027. The latest government report underscores both the urgency and the scale of the effort. More than 3,300 people have been vaccinated in North Kivu, leaving just 247 doses there and prompting an urgent request for 10,000 more. Researchers are also testing experimental treatments and post-exposure therapies as part of several trials. Those scientific advances may create another challenge. Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation, warned that financing and procurement arrangements need to be established before trial results arrive so that successful vaccines or medicines can quickly be manufactured and delivered at scale. “The measure of success of this outbreak response will not be whether new tools are developed, but whether those at risk can benefit from them,” said Charlotte Watts, Wellcome’s director of solutions. For now, however, the epidemic is still being fought largely with the basic tools of outbreak control: finding infected people, tracing their contacts, isolating patients, protecting health workers and persuading frightened communities to cooperate. Those measures can work. The difficulty is making them work simultaneously across a vast area affected by armed conflict and a health system that was struggling long before Ebola arrived. “This is an outbreak that with good public health measures can be controlled,” Clemmer said. “It’s just we need those measures” to overcome the systems problems standing in their way. news.content_original: Subscribe Digital Print November 18, 2026 Subscribe Digital Print Cyberattacks APEC Foreign community in Japan Latest News Today's print edition Home Delivery JAPAN Politics Society Crime & Legal Science & Health Explainer History WORLD Politics Crime & Legal Science & Health Society ASIA PACIFIC Politics Crime & Legal Science & Health Society BUSINESS Companies Economy Markets Tech SPORTS Sumo Soccer Baseball Basketball Tennis Olympics More sports OPINION Editorials Commentary Geoeconomic Briefing Environment CLIMATE CHANGE Energy SUSTAINABILITY WILDLIFE EARTH SCIENCE LIFE Travel Digital Food & Drink Style & Design Language Lifestyle CULTURE Film Books Music Art TV & Streaming Stage Entertainment news COMMUNITY Voices Issues How-tos Our Lives My Account My Bookmarks Logout Subscribe for more access WORLD / Science & Health Ebola outbreak defies control as war and hunger fuel crisis six months in People pass through at an Ebola health checkpoint on the outskirts of Biakato, Congo, a small town deep in the rainforest which now accounts for as many as one-quarter of the sprawling country’s new Ebola cases, on Oct. 19. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times BLOOMBERG SHARE/SAVE X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link Nov 16, 2026 Listen to this article 7 min Six months into the biggest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s history, containing the virus increasingly depends on solving problems far beyond Ebola — hunger, armed conflict, mistrust and a health system already buckling under the strain. More than 11,000 people have been infected and 5,500 have died since the outbreak was declared May 15. For months, Ebola has been killing roughly 240 people a week, the equivalent of about one and a half Boeing Co. 737 passenger jets crashing every week. “It’s a systems problem compounded by basically geography, insecurity, conflict, poor roads, mistrust,” said William Clemmer, a physician who has worked in Congo for three decades and is senior regional health adviser for Corus International based in Goma. Clemmer, 69, who has worked on four Ebola outbreaks, said many health facilities entered the current crisis without reliable water, electricity, sterilization, waste disposal or supply systems. Delivering protective equipment can only accomplish so much if clinics lack the basic infrastructure needed to use it safely, he said. Congo’s own data illustrate the problem. As of Nov. 14, the country had recorded 11,376 confirmed infections and 5,568 deaths, for a fatality rate of almost 49%. The outbreak had reached 68 health zones across eight provinces. In North Kivu province, 153 Ebola patients and suspected cases were being cared for in ordinary health facilities outside designated treatment and isolation centers on Nov. 14. People who aren’t identified and isolated can continue spreading Ebola at home, in clinics and during funerals. A local shop keeper is helped at a makeshift treatment center for Ebola patients in Biakato, Congo, on Oct. 16. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times About two-thirds of Ebola deaths have recently occurred in communities rather than treatment centers, according to Medecins Sans Frontieres. “When two-thirds of our deaths occur in local communities, that basically tells us that either people are being detected too late or they’re not reaching care at all,” Clemmer said. “That is an indication not just of failure of surveillance, but also of access, trust and security.” Fear factor The International Rescue Committee said its teams recently documented 84 rumors, including a recurring belief that people taken to Ebola treatment centers “do not return home alive.” The group said fear is discouraging some women from seeking routine medical care, including postnatal services. The outbreak’s roughly 50% fatality rate makes that reluctance understandable, Clemmer said. Unlike the 2018-2020 Ebola epidemic in eastern Congo, responders don’t yet have a vaccine or treatment proven to work against the Bundibugyo strain driving the current outbreak. Telling families that a relative needs to enter a treatment center where many patients are dying can fuel resistance, he said. The consequences extend far beyond Ebola. Almost 29 million people in Congo already face acute food insecurity, a number projected to exceed 30 million in the first half of next year, according to United Nations agencies. More than 11 million of them are in Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu, the eastern provinces at the center of the country’s humanitarian crisis. Conflict displaces families from their farms and livelihoods, while Ebola restrictions and fear can further disrupt farming and trade. For health officials, that creates another obstacle: asking someone exposed to Ebola to isolate is harder when leaving home may be necessary to earn money or find food. “These people have the responsibility of working, of getting food for their family,” Clemmer said. Violence poses a more direct threat, with armed groups killing more people than Ebola itself in some affected areas, Julien Harneis, the U.N.’s senior Ebola response coordinator, said last week. Health care workers carry the corpse of a victim from a makeshift Ebola treatment center in Biakato, Congo on Oct. 18. | Daniel Berehulak / The New York Times Over one recent weekend, more people were murdered by the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) than died from the virus, he said in a post marking six months since the outbreak was declared. The violence is also making the epidemic harder to stop. Harneis said one of the response’s most pressing challenges is finding ways to improve contact tracing in conflict areas where attacks by the ADF and other armed groups are impeding the work. He also called for greater engagement with private health providers, where he said most people initially seek care. Scientific hope There are reasons for optimism. Transmission has declined in some former hotspots, neighboring countries have so far avoided sustained spread, and clinical trials under way in Congo could eventually provide vaccines and treatments specifically suited to Bundibugyo Ebola. Thousands of people are already receiving Merck & Co.’s Ervebo vaccine while scientists investigate whether the shot, approved against Zaire ebolavirus, can also protect against Bundibugyo. Africa CDC said emerging evidence suggests it may provide some cross-protection and supports its use in high-risk children while the evaluation continues. Meanwhile, two vaccines designed specifically against Bundibugyo — one developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India and another from Moderna — are set to enter a late-stage trial in Congo. Researchers will test whether they can protect people exposed to the virus from developing severe disease or dying, with results expected in early 2027. The latest government report underscores both the urgency and the scale of the effort. More than 3,300 people have been vaccinated in North Kivu, leaving just 247 doses there and prompting an urgent request for 10,000 more. Researchers are also testing experimental treatments and post-exposure therapies as part of several trials. Those scientific advances may create another challenge. Wellcome, a London-based health research foundation, warned that financing and procurement arrangements need to be established before trial results arrive so that successful vaccines or medicines can quickly be manufactured and delivered at scale. “The measure of success of this outbreak response will not be whether new tools are developed, but whether those at risk can benefit from them,” said Charlotte Watts, Wellcome’s director of solutions. For now, however, the epidemic is still being fought largely with the basic tools of outbreak control: finding infected people, tracing their contacts, isolating patients, protecting health workers and persuading frightened communities to cooperate. Those measures can work. The difficulty is making them work simultaneously across a vast area affected by armed conflict and a health system that was struggling long before Ebola arrived. “This is an outbreak that with good public health measures can be controlled,” Clemmer said. “It’s just we need those measures” to overcome the systems problems standing in their way. analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 由于冲突和不安全局势,卫生官员正在努力追踪接触者和隔离工作。暴发 正在通过使用默克公司的 Ervebo 疫苗 得到解决,该药物被批准用于扎伊尔埃博拉病毒,并且针对 Bundibugyo 特异性 疫苗 的临床试验正在进行中。恐惧、不信任以及在冲突地区提供护理的挑战也阻碍了应对工作。

analysis.brief_en: Africa CDC issued a statement on November 15, 2026, regarding US travel restrictions related to the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak. The statement highlights the organization's role in supporting the Democratic Republic of the Congo government to enhance transparency and accountability in Ebola response funding. It also outlines broader initiatives such as the Africa’s Health Security and Sovereignty (AHSS) agenda, which aims to empower African nations to finance and govern their health systems. However, the evidence does not provide specific details on the outbreak's scale, impact, or risk level. The statement is part of a larger context of public health efforts and does not include confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures. The response status is under investigation, with no further details on the outbreak's current status or containment measures.

news.content_title: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into response
news.content: FILE PHOTO: Congolese medical workers wearing personal protective equipment carry the wooden coffin containing the body of Dr Marie-France Shogogo, who died at an Ebola treatment centre after contracting the virus, as aid agencies intensify efforts to contain a new Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus, during her burial under specialized safe and dignified burial protocols at Nyamurongo Cemetery in Bunia town, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, on Oct. 31, 2026. Photo by Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering. More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016. READ MORE: Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year. By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire. New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system. Questions over funding and management Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities. One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment. Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for. "A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues," said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF. Children face high death rates Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say. Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates. According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died. Conflict and attacks hamper response Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices. Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack. The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict. READ MORE: Inside the study for a remedy to fight Congo's deadliest Ebola outbreak Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians. The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record. analysis.brief_en: An Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control six months into the response. Over 11,000 cases have been recorded, with nearly half of the infected individuals dying, according to government data. This outbreak is the deadliest in Congo's history, surpassing the death toll from the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 80% of new cases are detected outside official health surveillance, indicating widespread undetected circulation. Community transmission is high, with 35% of deaths among children and nearly 72% of infected children under 5 succumbing to the disease. The virus has spread to eight provinces, and fears of continent-wide transmission persist. Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, are inadequate, and health workers have gone on strike due to unpaid wages. Over $700 million in aid remains unaccounted for, and conflict in the region has further complicated response efforts.

Over 11,000 cases have been recorded, with nearly half of the infected individuals dying, according to government data. This outbreak is the deadliest in Congo's history, surpassing the death toll from the West African outbreak between 2014 and 2016. Community transmission is high, with 35% of deaths among children and nearly 72% of infected children under 5 succumbing to the disease. The virus has spread to eight provinces, and fears of continent-wide transmission persist. Over $700 million in aid remains unaccounted for, and conflict in the region has further complicated response efforts.

news.content: Health World Africa 3,000 recover from Ebola in DR Congo: WHO Since May, over 11,000 confirmed cases, including 5,400 deaths, have been recorded, according to official data James Tasamba 15 November 2026 • Update : 15 November 2026 KIGALI, Rwanda About 3,000 people have recovered from Ebola virus disease in the Democratic Republic of Congo and returned home, thanks to the efforts of health workers, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Sunday, as the country battles its largest outbreak on record. World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus expressed deep gratitude to the nurses, doctors, community health workers, contact tracers and burial teams who he said are working under extraordinary pressure to save lives. "Amid immense hardship, local responders and global partners, under the leadership of the government, are driving hard-won progress. Transmission is slowing in several early epicentres, and clinical trials, including the Tumaini trial and new vaccine candidates, are advancing rapidly," Tedros said in a post on the US social media platform X. WHO declared the Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus in Congo a public health emergency of international concern six months ago. Since then, more than 11,000 confirmed cases, including 5,400 deaths, have been recorded in 67 health zones across eight provinces. Tedros called for safe humanitarian access and a cessation of hostilities so health workers can reach every affected area without fear. Noting that ending Ebola starts and ends with communities, Tedros urged Ebola responders to build trust through listening, respect and compassionate care so people seek treatment early, when lives can be saved. He urged donors to step up and close critical funding gaps to sustain the response, saying WHO would remain steadfast in its support for the people of Congo, working with the government and partners until zero cases remain. Earlier this month, Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) Director-General Jean Kaseya said two-thirds of the $2.9 billion in funding mobilized for the Ebola response on the continent had yet to be disbursed. Congo’s Ebola Outbreak Is Spreading Faster Than Ever — and Killing at Record Pace The Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains uncontrolled six months after its declaration, with increasing case numbers and deaths. Newsroom November 17, 2026 Facebook X WhatsApp Linkedin ReddIt Telegram A Congolese hygiene worker wearing personal protective equipment (PPE) takes measurements at a red-zone where patients were declared cured of Ebola virus disease at the International Medical Corps (IMC) Ebola treatment center, at the Beni General Referral Hospital, as aid agencies intensify efforts to contain the Ebola outbreak involving the Bundibugyo strain, in Beni, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, November 16, 2026. REUTERS/Gradel Muyisa Mumbere The Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo remains uncontrolled six months after its declaration, with increasing case numbers and deaths. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, is spreading more rapidly than any previous outbreak, with over 11,000 infected and more than 5,500 deaths reported since May 15. Infections and fatalities are rising at twice the rate seen during the first six months of the West Africa outbreak in 2014-16, which was the largest on record. This is Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak, surpassing the previous largest outbreak from 2018-2020. Security issues and poor coordination are major challenges, with health workers facing attacks and communities skeptical of outsiders. There are reports of health workers striking over unpaid salaries, slowing the response. While $2.9 billion has been pledged for managing the outbreak, less than half has been released. The World Health Organization urges donors to collaborate with the Congolese government to ensure effective use of resources. With information from Reuters Stay ahead of the geopolitical week. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, is spreading more rapidly than any previous outbreak, with over 11,000 infected and more than 5,500 deaths reported since May 15. Learn more Publications ⚲ Back to news Statements Access planning for Ebola medicines moves ahead during clinical trials Gilead’s newly announced voluntary licenses could speed access to medicines currently under evaluation for treatment and prevention of Ebola BDV, as Unitaid and partners advance access roadmaps to help affected countries secure supplies if trials are successful. 17 November 2026 © WHO Unitaid welcomes Gilead’s announcement of royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories. The agreements lay the groundwork for wider access to obeldesivir, an investigational antiviral being studied to prevent Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). If clinical evidence supports its use and regulators approve it, the three manufacturers across different regions will be able to produce and supply obeldesivir in the 127 countries covered by the licenses. Gilead is also expanding its existing licenses for remdesivir – an antiviral used to treat COVID-19 – to cover Ebola BVD, paving the way for wider access pending clinical trial results. While clinical trials are still underway, Unitaid, WHO, countries, regional and international partners in the Ebola response have developed access roadmaps for candidate Ebola BVD medicines, including obeldesivir and remdesivir. These roadmaps identify the steps stakeholders can take now to help countries secure supplies quickly when and if the medicines are proven to work. As part of this effort, Unitaid is leading the engagement with manufacturers of these two antivirals to secure access commitments to supply all countries in need. Through its funded programs, Unitaid is also supporting and anticipating interventions to prepare for supply and adoption of therapeutics and diagnostics so countries can introduce these key tools without delay if trials support their use. analysis.location_and_population: Global, with focus on 127 countries covered by the licenses.
analysis.event: Unitaid and partners are advancing access planning for candidate Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) medicines, including obeldesivir and remdesivir, during ongoing clinical trials. The event is confirmed based on the announcement by Unitaid and Gilead.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The initiative aims to secure supply commitments for obeldesivir and remdesivir in 127 countries if clinical trials support their use. No specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Access roadmaps are being developed for candidate medicines, and Gilead is expanding licenses for remdesivir to cover Ebola BVD. Clinical trials are ongoing, and regulatory approval is pending. The response is under investigation and preparation.

analysis.brief_en: Unitaid and its partners are advancing access planning for candidate medicines to treat Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), including obeldesivir and remdesivir, during ongoing clinical trials. The initiative involves securing supply commitments from manufacturers across different regions to ensure availability in 127 countries if trials prove effective. Gilead has announced royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma, and Ferozsons Laboratories, which will allow production and distribution of obeldesivir if approved. Additionally, Gilead is expanding its existing licenses for remdesivir, an antiviral used for COVID-19, to cover BVD. These efforts are part of broader strategies to prepare for potential supply and adoption of therapeutics and diagnostics, ensuring countries can introduce these tools without delay if clinical evidence supports their use. The progress is reported as of November 17, 2026, and is based on the collaboration between Unitaid, WHO, and other stakeholders in the Ebola response.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 18, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Uganda Outpaced Congo in Standing Ebola Preparedness Before the 2026 Outbreak by November 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Uganda Outpaced Congo in Standing Ebola Preparedness Before the 2026 Outbreak Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram When the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak emerged simultaneously across international borders on May 15, 2026, the public health systems of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda confronted an identical pathogen with no licensed vaccines or established therapeutic cures. A comprehensive scoping review published in Infectious Diseases of Poverty by an international research team led by Augustus Osborne indicates that pre-existing national preparedness policy architecture and standing health system capabilities differed substantially between the two sovereign nations long before the pathogen surfaced. By rigorously evaluating national policy instruments in force at the outbreak onset alongside external international assessments, the authors identified marked disparities in baseline surveillance, institutional accountability, displaced population inclusion, and standing isolation infrastructure, providing critical documentary evidence for how pre-crisis health security structures may condition operational epidemic response. The investigative team framed their scoping inquiry around the standardized methodologies of the Arksey and O’Malley framework, refined by Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and documented in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. Because the primary objective was to map a heterogeneous body of legal statutes, national health sector strategies, multi-hazard emergency guidelines, and independent technical evaluations rather than calculate a single pooled statistical effect size, the researchers retrieved fifty-seven verified sources following rigorous bibliographic checking. The evidentiary corpus encompassed fifteen national policy instruments in force on May 15, 2026—six originating from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and nine from Uganda—alongside seventeen operational outbreak records, International Health Regulations evaluation dossiers, and regional framework agreements. Each country’s standing instruments were searched, extracted, and charted against fifty-two detailed component requirements grouped into ten substantive governance and health system dimensions, with an eleventh dimension measuring operational specificity. A predetermined synthesis rule scored the coverage and modal specificity of each dimension into four categorical descriptors: adequate, partially adequate, inadequate, or absent. Across the fifty-two standardized preparedness components, Uganda’s legal and strategic policy instruments addressed forty-seven requirements, representing an overall national coverage rate of 90.4 percent, whereas the national instruments of the Democratic Republic of the Congo addressed thirty-eight components, yielding a coverage rate of 73.1 percent. When the research team evaluated the operational specificity of the individual policy provisions, the disparity became even more pronounced. Highly specific provisions—defined as concrete policy stipulations identifying responsible institutions, enforceable timelines, and quantified logistical resources—constituted 31.7 percent of Uganda’s 142 charted provisions, compared to just 15.2 percent of the 66 provisions charted from Congolese instruments. Conversely, provisions exhibiting low specificity, defined as aspirational intentions or generic assertions lacking procedural grounding, made up 15.5 percent of Uganda’s provisions but comprised 45.5 percent of the Congolese texts. Under the study’s standardized scoring metric, Uganda achieved higher policy ratings than the Democratic Republic of the Congo in six dimensions, including surveillance, isolation capacity, displaced populations, accountability, alignment with international standards, and operational specificity, while neither country was rated higher than the other in the remaining five dimensions. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Track Outbreaks Buy Maps Read Travel Guides Surveillance architecture demonstrated the widest technical gap in standing operational specificity between the two sovereign neighbors. Uganda’s instruments addressed six of the seven surveillance components, supported by twenty-nine individual provisions of which twelve were ranked as highly specific. The country’s National Action Plan for Health Security outlined year-by-year modular training schedules in integrated disease surveillance and response, designated seven functional national reference laboratories, and mandated organized diagnostic specimen transport networks across at least 80 percent of administrative districts. Furthermore, Uganda’s strategic health framework established strict performance targets requiring detection of emergencies within 72 hours and laboratory confirmation within seven days, while operational guidelines for regional public health emergency operations centers instituted mandatory daily reporting aligned with the 7-1-7 timeliness standard. Although the Democratic Republic of the Congo also addressed six of the seven surveillance components in its multi-hazard emergency management plan, eight of its thirteen charted surveillance provisions exhibited low specificity, offering no operational case definitions and no enforceable timeliness metrics for electronic disease notification. Standing capacities for case isolation and clinical care revealed severe logistical deficits that materialized as acute operational challenges once community transmission accelerated. While neither nation had formally established minimum per-capita isolation bed allocations or standing surge deployment triggers in pre-existing statutes, their documented material commitments varied substantially. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the pre-existing national multi-hazard emergency plan quantified a theoretical national requirement of specialized case-management kits for 500 patients, but explicitly recorded that zero kits were physically available in national stockpiles at baseline. In contrast, Uganda’s policy provisions prioritized pre-positioning critical containment supplies across regional referral hospitals and detailed institutional mechanisms for specialized patient conveyance and dedicated ambulance routing. The integration of forcibly displaced communities into national health emergency architectures proved to be an equally decisive technical contrast between the two countries. Prior to the epidemic, June 2026 humanitarian assessments indicated that more than two million internally displaced people resided within Congolese administrative zones at direct risk from the pathogen, while Uganda hosted over two million refugees and asylum seekers, roughly one-third of whom were Congolese nationals. Uganda’s dedicated Health Sector Integrated Refugee Response Plan comprehensively addressed all five standardized evaluation components with high operational specificity, institutionalizing settlement health data into the centralized national health information system, funding community health workers within host districts, and formally embedding refugee emergency coordination under joint ministerial and United Nations governance. In stark contrast, Congolese emergency instruments addressed only two components, treating internal displacement as an isolated domestic hazard managed through the Ministry of the Interior rather than integrating displacement camp clinics into active epidemic surveillance networks. Despite widespread differences across domestic sectors, both nations exhibited critical, shared vulnerabilities in cross-border health governance and investigational medical countermeasure readiness. Neither country maintained standing bilateral protocols establishing binding cross-border case notification timelines, nor had either established standardized epidemiological thresholds to govern international movement restrictions with humanitarian protections. In the absence of bilateral legal treaties, Uganda enacted a unilateral suspension of international passenger transit across the border, an emergency measure contrary to temporary recommendations under the International Health Regulations and guidance issued by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Regarding medical countermeasures, neither government possessed a standing regulatory instrument addressing Bundibugyo virus disease, as available vaccines and licensed monoclonal antibody therapies were specific solely to Zaire ebolavirus. However, Uganda possessed an established domestic approval framework linking institutional review boards, the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology, and the National Drug Authority under an emergency compassionate-use protocol, enabling rapid clinical deployment of investigational remdesivir, whereas the Democratic Republic of the Congo initiated its first experimental clinical trial on July 2. Independent multilateral health security evaluations conducted prior to the outbreak strongly mirrored the researchers’ documentary policy findings. The Joint External Evaluation missions executed under the auspices of the World Health Organization in October 2023 utilized an identical fifty-six indicator metric across both countries, awarding Uganda a mean overall technical capacity score of 2.75 points compared to 1.63 points for the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This represented a statistically robust mean paired difference of 1.13 points, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.83 to 1.42 points and a Wilcoxon signed-rank significance of P less than 0.001. Uganda scored higher across forty individual indicators, scored identically on thirteen, and scored lower on only three, with infection prevention and control representing the sole technical area where Congolese baseline scores exceeded Ugandan metrics. The largest institutional divergences emerged within national health emergency management, where Uganda averaged 3.50 against the Congo’s 1.17, and designated points of entry, where Uganda averaged 3.33 compared to 1.33. Similarly, self-reported capacity scores under the States Parties Self-Assessment Annual Reporting mechanism consistently favored Uganda by 16 to 31 percentage points between 2018 and 2025. A critical analytical contribution of the review lies in examining the reactive One Health response plan issued by the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s National Institute of Public Health on May 29, 2026, two weeks following the official outbreak declaration. Unlike the country’s ambiguous standing multi-hazard framework, this targeted provincial response plan covered thirty-seven of the fifty-two standardized components and achieved high operational specificity across 56.8 percent of its provisions. The reactive instrument clearly delineated four epidemiological caseload scenarios, established an aggressive 12-hour laboratory diagnostic standard, planned specialized ambulance allocations for each affected health zone, and guaranteed frontline staff financial allowances. The authors argue that this sharp contrast indicates the Democratic Republic of the Congo possessed sophisticated technical competencies in post-declaration emergency planning, but suffered from profound deficits in the enduring, permanent health system arrangements that must be financed, legally codified, and structurally maintained during non-epidemic periods, such as functional statutory emergency operations centers, quarantine laws, and standing material stockpiles. While the study demonstrates significant structural alignment between pre-existing policy completeness and subsequent containment outcomes, the authors emphasize essential methodological limitations inherent to documentary health systems research. A scoping review of policy documents and evaluation reports describes what institutional instruments mandate rather than verifying day-to-day implementation fidelity or frontline clinical efficacy across peripheral health centers. Furthermore, documented policy variations cannot be interpreted as the sole or definitive cause of the different outbreak trajectories, as significant unmeasured external confounders—including intense armed conflict, community distrust, remote geography, and prolonged undetected viral circulation prior to official notification—heavily shaped the operating environment in eastern Congo. The authors conclude that immediate health security reforms must prioritize establishing statutory emergency authorities, enforceable surveillance standards, and linked humanitarian health networks within the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while both nations must formalize standing cross-border governance protocols and pre-approved clinical pathways for investigational medical countermeasures. S., Bangura, C., & Sesay, U. (2026).
