Because the primary objective was to map a heterogeneous body of legal statutes, national health sector strategies, multi-hazard emergency guidelines, and independent technical evaluations rather than calculate a single pooled statistical effect size, the researchers retrieved fifty-seven verified sources following rigorous bibliographic checking. The evidentiary corpus encompassed fifteen national policy instruments in force on May 15, 2026—six originating from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and nine from Uganda—alongside seventeen operational outbreak records, International Health Regulations evaluation dossiers, and regional framework agreements. Each country’s standing instruments were searched, extracted, and charted against fifty-two detailed component requirements grouped into ten substantive governance and health system dimensions, with an eleventh dimension measuring operational specificity. A predetermined synthesis rule scored the coverage and modal specificity of each dimension into four categorical descriptors: adequate, partially adequate, inadequate, or absent. Across the fifty-two standardized preparedness components, Uganda’s legal and strategic policy instruments addressed forty-seven requirements, representing an overall national coverage rate of 90.4 percent, whereas the national instruments of the Democratic Republic of the Congo addressed thirty-eight components, yielding a coverage rate of 73.1 percent. When the research team evaluated the operational specificity of the individual policy provisions, the disparity became even more pronounced. Highly specific provisions—defined as concrete policy stipulations identifying responsible institutions, enforceable timelines, and quantified logistical resources—constituted 31.7 percent of Uganda’s 142 charted provisions, compared to just 15.2 percent of the 66 provisions charted from Congolese instruments. Conversely, provisions exhibiting low specificity, defined as aspirational intentions or generic assertions lacking procedural grounding, made up 15.5 percent of Uganda’s provisions but comprised 45.5 percent of the Congolese texts. Under the study’s standardized scoring metric, Uganda achieved higher policy ratings than the Democratic Republic of the Congo in six dimensions, including surveillance, isolation capacity, displaced populations, accountability, alignment with international standards, and operational specificity, while neither country was rated higher than the other in the remaining five dimensions. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Track Outbreaks Buy Maps Read Travel Guides Surveillance architecture demonstrated the widest technical gap in standing operational specificity between the two sovereign neighbors. Uganda’s instruments addressed six of the seven surveillance components, supported by twenty-nine individual provisions of which twelve were ranked as highly specific. The country’s National Action Plan for Health Security outlined year-by-year modular training schedules in integrated disease surveillance and response, designated seven functional national reference laboratories, and mandated organized diagnostic specimen transport networks across at least 80 percent of administrative districts. Furthermore, Uganda’s strategic health framework established strict performance targets requiring detection of emergencies within 72 hours and laboratory confirmation within seven days, while operational guidelines for regional public health emergency operations centers instituted mandatory daily reporting aligned with the 7-1-7 timeliness standard. Although the Democratic Republic of the Congo also addressed six of the seven surveillance components in its multi-hazard emergency management plan, eight of its thirteen charted surveillance provisions exhibited low specificity, offering no operational case definitions and no enforceable timeliness metrics for electronic disease notification. Standing capacities for case isolation and clinical care revealed severe logistical deficits that materialized as acute operational challenges once community transmission accelerated. While neither nation had formally established minimum per-capita isolation bed allocations or standing surge deployment triggers in pre-existing statutes, their documented material commitments varied substantially. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the pre-existing national multi-hazard emergency plan quantified a theoretical national requirement of specialized case-management kits for 500 patients, but explicitly recorded that zero kits were physically available in national stockpiles at baseline. In contrast, Uganda’s policy provisions prioritized pre-positioning critical containment supplies across regional referral hospitals and detailed institutional mechanisms for specialized patient conveyance and dedicated ambulance routing. The integration of forcibly displaced communities into national health emergency architectures proved to be an equally decisive technical contrast between the two countries. Prior to the epidemic, June 2026 humanitarian assessments indicated that more than two million internally displaced people resided within Congolese administrative zones at direct risk from the pathogen, while Uganda hosted over two million refugees and asylum seekers, roughly one-third of whom were Congolese nationals. Uganda’s dedicated Health Sector Integrated Refugee Response Plan comprehensively addressed all five standardized evaluation components with high operational specificity, institutionalizing settlement health data into the centralized national health information system, funding community health workers within host districts, and formally embedding refugee emergency coordination under joint ministerial and United Nations governance. In stark contrast, Congolese emergency instruments addressed only two components, treating internal displacement as an isolated domestic hazard managed through the Ministry of the Interior rather than integrating displacement camp clinics into active epidemic surveillance networks. Despite widespread differences across domestic sectors, both nations exhibited critical, shared vulnerabilities in cross-border health governance and investigational medical countermeasure readiness. Neither country maintained standing bilateral protocols establishing binding cross-border case notification timelines, nor had either established standardized epidemiological thresholds to govern international movement restrictions with humanitarian protections. In the absence of bilateral legal treaties, Uganda enacted a unilateral suspension of international passenger transit across the border, an emergency measure contrary to temporary recommendations under the International Health Regulations and guidance issued by the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Regarding medical countermeasures, neither government possessed a standing regulatory instrument addressing Bundibugyo virus disease, as available vaccines and licensed monoclonal antibody therapies were specific solely to Zaire ebolavirus. However, Uganda possessed an established domestic approval framework linking institutional review boards, the Uganda National Council for Science and Technology, and the National Drug Authority under an emergency compassionate-use protocol, enabling rapid clinical deployment of investigational remdesivir, whereas the Democratic Republic of the Congo initiated its first experimental clinical trial on July 2. Independent multilateral health security evaluations conducted prior to the outbreak strongly mirrored the researchers’ documentary policy findings. The Joint External Evaluation missions executed under the auspices of the World Health Organization in October 2023 utilized an identical fifty-six indicator metric across both countries, awarding Uganda a mean overall technical capacity score of 2.75 points compared to 1.63 points for the Democratic Republic of the Congo. This represented a statistically robust mean paired difference of 1.13 points, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 0.83 to 1.42 points and a Wilcoxon signed-rank significance of P less than 0.001. Uganda scored higher across forty individual indicators, scored identically on thirteen, and scored lower on only three, with infection prevention and control representing the sole technical area where Congolese baseline scores exceeded Ugandan metrics. The largest institutional divergences emerged within national health emergency management, where Uganda averaged 3.50 against the Congo’s 1.17, and designated points of entry, where Uganda averaged 3.33 compared to 1.33. Similarly, self-reported capacity scores under the States Parties Self-Assessment Annual Reporting mechanism consistently favored Uganda by 16 to 31 percentage points between 2018 and 2025. A critical analytical contribution of the review lies in examining the reactive One Health response plan issued by the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s National Institute of Public Health on May 29, 2026, two weeks following the official outbreak declaration. Unlike the country’s ambiguous standing multi-hazard framework, this targeted provincial response plan covered thirty-seven of the fifty-two standardized components and achieved high operational specificity across 56.8 percent of its provisions. The reactive instrument clearly delineated four epidemiological caseload scenarios, established an aggressive 12-hour laboratory diagnostic standard, planned specialized ambulance allocations for each affected health zone, and guaranteed frontline staff financial allowances. The authors argue that this sharp contrast indicates the Democratic Republic of the Congo possessed sophisticated technical competencies in post-declaration emergency planning, but suffered from profound deficits in the enduring, permanent health system arrangements that must be financed, legally codified, and structurally maintained during non-epidemic periods, such as functional statutory emergency operations centers, quarantine laws, and standing material stockpiles. While the study demonstrates significant structural alignment between pre-existing policy completeness and subsequent containment outcomes, the authors emphasize essential methodological limitations inherent to documentary health systems research. A scoping review of policy documents and evaluation reports describes what institutional instruments mandate rather than verifying day-to-day implementation fidelity or frontline clinical efficacy across peripheral health centers. Furthermore, documented policy variations cannot be interpreted as the sole or definitive cause of the different outbreak trajectories, as significant unmeasured external confounders—including intense armed conflict, community distrust, remote geography, and prolonged undetected viral circulation prior to official notification—heavily shaped the operating environment in eastern Congo. The authors conclude that immediate health security reforms must prioritize establishing statutory emergency authorities, enforceable surveillance standards, and linked humanitarian health networks within the Democratic Republic of the Congo, while both nations must formalize standing cross-border governance protocols and pre-approved clinical pathways for investigational medical countermeasures. analysis.event: A scoping review published in Infectious Diseases of Poverty compared the preparedness policies of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo before the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The study identified significant differences in their health system capabilities and policy frameworks.

analysis.brief_en: A scoping review published in Infectious Diseases of Poverty compared the preparedness policies of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo before the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The study, led by Augustus Osborne, found that Uganda had a more robust policy framework, addressing 47 out of 52 preparedness components (90.4% coverage) compared to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which addressed 38 (73.1% coverage). Uganda's policies included specific measures such as modular training schedules, national reference laboratories, and diagnostic specimen transport networks. The research emphasized the importance of pre-crisis health security structures in shaping epidemic response, noting significant gaps in operational specificity and logistical readiness, particularly in surveillance and isolation capacities. The findings were based on a thorough analysis of national policy instruments, outbreak records, and international assessments, without direct testing or investigation of the outbreak itself.

news.source_body_en: A scoping review published in Infectious Diseases of Poverty compared the preparedness policies of Uganda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo before the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. The study, led by Augustus Osborne, found that Uganda had a more robust policy framework, addressing 47 out of 52 preparedness components (90.4% coverage) compared to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which addressed 38 (73.1% coverage). Uganda's policies included specific measures such as modular training schedules, national reference laboratories, and diagnostic specimen transport networks. The research emphasized the importance of pre-crisis health security structures in shaping epidemic response, noting significant gaps in operational specificity and logistical readiness, particularly in surveillance and isolation capacities. The findings were based on a thorough analysis of national policy instruments, outbreak records, and international assessments, without direct testing or investigation of the outbreak itself.
news.content_zh: 《传染病与贫困》中发表的一篇范围界定审查比较了乌干达和刚果民主共和国在 2026 年本迪布焦病毒病 暴发 之前的防备政策。由 Augustus Osborne 领导的这项研究发现,乌干达拥有更健全的政策框架,解决了 52 个准备部分中的 47 个(覆盖率 90.4%),而刚果民主共和国则解决了 38 个(覆盖率 73.1%)。乌干达的政策包括具体措施,例如模块化培训计划、国家参考实验室和诊断标本运输网络。该研究强调了危机前卫生安全结构在制定流行病应对措施方面的重要性,并指出在行动特异性和后勤准备情况方面存在巨大差距,特别是在 监测 和隔离能力方面。研究结果基于对国家政策工具、暴发 记录和国际评估的彻底分析,没有对 暴发 本身进行直接测试或调查。

Technology transfer planning has begun with three named manufacturers, and additional partners are being pursued to expand capacity before confirmatory clinical and regulatory milestones. The Ebo-pep Phase III randomized, placebo-controlled field trial is evaluating post-exposure prophylaxis efficacy in high-risk contacts during active outbreaks, coordinated by ALIMA and collaborators. Remdesivir has been donated for investigational/compassionate use in multiple countries, while separate WHO-sponsored Partners trial data may inform potential remdesivir labeling for Ebola BVD. SHOW MORE Gilead signs royalty-free licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to expand future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir. Advertisement The expanded access will also include the previously existing Remdesivir agreements. Stock.Adobe.com Gilead Sciences signed royalty-free voluntary licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis for Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease. The agreements will cover 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, including all African countries that have reported cases during the current Ebola BVD outbreak.1 The move signals Gilead’s effort to get ahead of a currently ongoing outbreak by lining up manufacturing and supply capacity before clinical results are even in. The geographic scope of the new agreements mirrors Gilead’s existing voluntary licensing arrangements for remdesivir in Covid-19, with the agreements being designed to support manufacturing readiness, technology transfer, and supply planning, while a field trial evaluating obeldesivir continues.1 What do the agreements cover? The royalty-free licenses allow Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma, and Ferozsons Laboratories to manufacture and supply obeldesivir in the licensed territory, contingent on clinical data and applicable regulatory authorizations.1 Technology transfer discussions are already underway with these three manufacturers, with Gilead saying agreements with additional manufacturers are under discussion. Recommendations tailored to you Sign in or create an account to see articles, videos, and podcasts matched to your specialties. Sign in or sign up What trial is evaluating obeldesivir? Obeldesivir is currently being evaluated in the Ebo-pep trial, a partner-led Phase III randomized, placebo-controlled field trial coordinated by ALIMA and partners.2 The trial is evaluating the efficacy of obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis for individuals at high risk of developing Ebola BVD.2 Obeldesivir has previously been evaluated in clinical trials for Covid-19 and respiratory syncytial virus, in addition to its preclinical filovirus activity. Related Articles M&A Roundup: Johnson & Johnson Acquires Ollin Biosciences, Eli Lilly Acquires Calytrix Bio, AmyriAD Therpaeutics Acquires AD04 Alzheimers Program, Sanofi Enters Collaboration with Seawolf Therapeutics Roundup: BioMarin Licenses Long-Acting Fabry Enzyme Therapy for $70 Million Upfront, Ferring to Acquire Fertility Biotech Gameto in Deal Worth Up to $1.38 Billion Roundup: Astellas Licenses IL-12 Fusion Protein From Audax in Deal Worth Up to $1.34 Billion, EVERSANA Acquires Health Economics Firm Estima Scientific The drug is currently not approved for post-exposure prophylaxis of filovirus disease, or for any indication, in any country.1 Jaime McCoy, vice president, Gilead Patient Solutions, Gilead Sciences, says responding to emerging infectious diseases, including Ebola virus disease, requires not only scientific innovation, but also early planning and collaboration to help ensure that effective medicines can reach the people who need them as quickly as possible. He continues to say, “These agreements reflect our commitment to preparing for future access while clinical research is ongoing, so that we are better positioned to respond if these investigational medicines demonstrate benefit and gain regulatory approval.” How has Gilead already responded to the outbreak? Beyond the new licensing agreements, Gilead has made direct product donations tied to the current outbreak. The company has donated more than 2,000 vials of remdesivir to Kenya for investigational use as treatment and post-exposure prophylaxis for people with confirmed Ebola BVD or individuals with a close contact exposure.1 More broadly, as part of its response to the current outbreak, Gilead has provided compassionate use donations of remdesivir to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, and Kenya totaling more than 38,000 vials. These efforts sit within what Gilead describes as a broader approach to outbreak preparedness that includes clinical research, manufacturing and supply planning, technology transfer, and collaboration with governments, public health agencies and global health partners. The licensing announcement is one piece of a broader outbreak response. Gilead is also updating its existing voluntary licensing agreements for remdesivir to include filovirus disease, which would support potential future access should results from the ongoing World Health Organization-sponsored Partners trial support remdesivir’s use as a treatment for Ebola BVD, pending potential regulatory approvals.1 The clinical efficacy of remdesivir for the treatment of Ebola BVD has not been established, and remdesivir is not currently approved in any country for the treatment or prevention of the disease. analysis.location_and_population: 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, including all African countries that have reported cases during the current Ebola BVD outbreak.
analysis.event: Gilead Sciences signed royalty-free licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir as post-exposure prophylaxis for Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease. The Ebo-pep Phase III randomized, placebo-controlled field trial is evaluating post-exposure prophylaxis efficacy in high-risk contacts during active outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The agreements aim to expand access to obeldesivir in 127 countries, with the drug currently not approved for post-exposure prophylaxis of filovirus disease or any indication in any country. Remdesivir has been donated for investigational/compassionate use in multiple countries, but its clinical efficacy for Ebola BVD has not been established.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Gilead has initiated technology transfer planning with three manufacturers and is pursuing additional partners to expand capacity. analysis.brief_en: Gilead Sciences has signed royalty-free licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers to support potential future access to its investigational antiviral obeldesivir for post-exposure prophylaxis of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease. These agreements cover 127 primarily low- and lower-middle-income countries, including all African nations reporting cases during the current outbreak. The Ebo-pep Phase III trial, coordinated by ALIMA and partners, is assessing obeldesivir's efficacy in high-risk contacts during active outbreaks. Gilead has also donated over 38,000 vials of remdesivir to Kenya, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Uganda for investigational use. While remdesivir has been donated for compassionate use, its clinical efficacy for Ebola BVD remains unconfirmed. The company is working to align manufacturing and supply readiness with ongoing clinical research and regulatory processes, signaling a proactive approach to outbreak preparedness. These efforts are part of a broader strategy to ensure effective medicines can reach those in need if they demonstrate benefit and gain regulatory approval.

The Ebo-pep Phase III trial, coordinated by ALIMA and partners, is assessing obeldesivir's efficacy in high-risk contacts during active outbreaks. While remdesivir has been donated for compassionate use, its clinical efficacy for Ebola BVD remains unconfirmed. The company is working to align manufacturing and supply readiness with ongoing clinical research and regulatory processes, signaling a proactive approach to outbreak preparedness. news.content_zh: 吉利德科学公司已与三个仿制药制造商签署了免版税许可协议,以支持未来可能获得其研究中的 抗病毒药物 奥贝地西韦,用于埃博拉本迪布焦病毒病的暴露后预防。这些协议主要覆盖 127 个低收入和中低收入国家,包括当前 暴发 期间报告病例的所有非洲国家。由 ALIMA 和合作伙伴协调的 Ebo-pep III 期试验正在评估奥贝昔韦在活跃 暴发 期间高风险接触者中的疗效。吉利德还向肯尼亚、刚果民主共和国和乌干达捐赠了 38,000 多瓶瑞德西韦用于研究用途。虽然瑞德西韦已被捐赠用于同情用途,但其对埃博拉 BVD 的临床疗效仍未得到证实。该公司正在努力使制造和供应准备与正在进行的临床研究和监管流程保持一致,这标志着 暴发 准备采取积极主动的方法。这些努力是更广泛战略的一部分,旨在确保有效药物在显示出益处并获得监管部门批准后能够惠及有需要的人。

news.content: Officially declared on 15 May, the Ebola epidemic affecting the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo ( DRC ) has continued to spread, reaching eight provinces across the country six months after it first emerged in Ituri. "We are all in agreement today to say that this outbreak is still serious, and is still not under control," Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention ( Africa CDC ), said on Sunday. In an interview with RFI , he described the outbreak as "extremely serious". More than 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths have been reported, according to government data. More than 80 percent of new cases are being detected among people who were not on contact-tracing lists, while over 65 percent of deaths occur in communities rather than healthcare facilities, Kaseya said. Ebola is most contagious during the late stages of the disease. "If we don't stop this outbreak now, it will be the worst Ebola outbreak that the world will have," he warned. A health worker wears full gear at a Ebola treatment camp in Butembo, Congo, Wednesday, on 30 September, 2026. While research into treatments and vaccines is progressing, efforts to contain the outbreak on the ground continue to face major obstacles. Driven by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus, the epidemic is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, after the 2014–2016 outbreak in West Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed over 11,000. Inside Bunia's fight to protect families from DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak The outbreak has also spread beyond the DRC over the past six months, reaching Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. " Uganda has managed to bring the epidemic under control," Kaseya explained. "We had declared its end there – even though two cases, one from Kenya and one from Nigeria, had passed through Uganda." The situation in Kenya has also improved. Last week, the country announced that the final patient had been discharged from facilities used to monitor people who had come into contact with infected individuals. "We have also seen very good results in Nigeria ," Kaseya added. "Not all the identified cases tested positive; at present, the situation appears to be under control." However, the Africa CDC chief remains concerned about the continuing spread of the epidemic within the DRC and the risk of further cross-border transmission. "First, there is the Central African Republic , which is a major source of concern for me. Second, there is South Sudan , which also remains a major source of concern." He also highlighted the potential risk to Rwanda and Burundi if the outbreak spreads from the Beni-Butembo area towards Goma and Bukavu. "And, of course, there are all the other countries that could be affected indirectly," he added. Medical charity warns funding for DRC Ebola fight not reaching front lines Kaseya told RFI that the lack of an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain remains one of the biggest challenges. A vaccine "should have been available for the past 19 years, given that the Bundibugyo strain has been known for that long," he said. He added that the absence of treatments and diagnostic tests specifically designed for the strain had contributed to the scale of the epidemic. Research into treatments and vaccines is progressing, however, with several clinical trials already underway, according to RFI's correspondent in Kinshasa, Paulina Zidi. The "Tumaini" clinical trial – named after the Swahili word for "hope" – is focusing on vaccine development. A group of experts from the World Health Organization ( WHO ) has recommended adding two new vaccine candidates specifically developed to target the Bundibugyo virus. Meanwhile, the Ebo-Pep trial is examining whether the oral antiviral drug obeldesivir can prevent the disease from developing in people exposed to the virus. The trial is being conducted at several locations, including treatment centres in Ituri managed by the medical NGO Alima . Africa CDC chief warns 'no country is safe' as Ebola reaches Nigeria Instability in eastern DRC, large-scale population movements and weaknesses in healthcare and disease surveillance have all contributed to the scale of the outbreak. Around $2.9 billion has been pledged internationally to help fight the epidemic. However, despite these commitments, much-needed assistance is still failing to reach some of the worst-affected areas, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières warned last week. The organisation highlighted shortages of trained staff, ambulances without fuel and a lack of surveillance teams. Kaseya acknowledged that coordination between the Congolese government and international donors remains a problem. "We are not pointing fingers," he said. "We are saying it's a collective failure." He called on donors to release around $1.6 billion in pledged aid and work more closely with Kinshasa to ensure funds are used effectively and resources are not wasted through duplication. Kaseya also acknowledged that some healthcare workers had not been paid for months, adding that the Congolese government was working to digitise its payroll system to address the problem. analysis.brief_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) remains out of control six months after its initial emergence in Ituri, according to the Africa CDC. Over 11,200 infections and 5,500 deaths have been reported, with more than 80 percent of new cases detected outside contact-tracing lists and over 65 percent of deaths occurring in communities rather than healthcare facilities. The outbreak, driven by the Bundibugyo strain, has spread to Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria, though these countries have managed to bring the epidemic under control. news.content: Breaking News Indian Envoy Visits Sneha Centre Stop Interfering, Stop Attacking Education Minister discusses cooperation with Arab Planning Institute Bahrain chairs 102nd GCC Olympic committees executive meeting Türkiye and ITU launch AI climate pledge at COP31 Indian Envoy Visits Sneha Centre Stop Interfering, Stop Attacking Education Minister discusses cooperation with Arab Planning Institute Bahrain chairs 102nd GCC Olympic committees executive meeting Türkiye and ITU launch AI climate pledge at COP31 Wednesday, 18 November 2026 عربيePaper News Views Videos ClassifiedsCampusCommunity More News Views Videos ClassifiedsCampusCommunity More SearchCtrl K Wednesday, 18 November 2026 Nov. 18 NewsViewsVideosClassifiedsCampusCommunity More NewsViewsVideosClassifiedsCampusCommunityMore Home News World 15 November 20265 min read New Ebola Vaccine and Treatment Trials Bring Hope in Congo Scientists are testing new vaccine candidates and experimental treatments against the deadly Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, as the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to battle a major outbreak. Aalia Quadir Published 15 November 2026, 11:37 Link copiedShare Save The search for effective vaccines and treatments against Ebola has entered a significant new phase, as international researchers advance clinical trials targeting the Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The latest developments offer renewed hope for affected communities, although scientists stress that further research is needed before any of the experimental options can be considered proven protection or treatment. On 4 November, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that two additional vaccine candidates had been recommended for evaluation in the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial. The candidates, ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469, are specifically designed to target the Bundibugyo virus. The recommendation represents an important development in the response, as these candidates are being considered for evaluation during an outbreak caused by the virus they were designed to target. Their entry into the trial is subject to national regulatory approvals. Two vaccine candidates enter the research pipeline The Tumaini trial is designed to evaluate multiple vaccine candidates through a single research platform. It uses a strategy known as ring vaccination, which focuses on identifying and enrolling people who have been in contact with confirmed Ebola patients. This approach aims to assess whether vaccination can help prevent illness and death among people at increased risk of exposure. The trial initially included Ervebo, an existing Ebola vaccine that has demonstrated effectiveness against the Zaire ebolavirus. However, its effectiveness against Bundibugyo virus remains unknown. The distinction is important because Ebola disease can be caused by different viruses, and protection demonstrated against one type cannot automatically be assumed to apply to another. According to WHO, four vaccination rings had already been established when it announced the latest recommendations, with additional rings being prepared. The inclusion of ChAdOx1 and mRNA-1469 is expected to expand the scientific investigation into potential protection against the Bundibugyo strain. Experimental treatments are also being investigated Alongside vaccine development, researchers are examining possible treatments for people already infected with the virus. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS clinical trial, which began enrolling patients in July 2026, is assessing whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral medicine remdesivir, or a combination of the two can improve survival among patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. WHO has also announced plans to add another potential treatment, maftivimab, to the trial. Separately, a study examining obeldevisir as a possible post-exposure preventive treatment is underway. These medicines remain investigational for Bundibugyo virus disease. Their effectiveness must be established through properly conducted clinical research before conclusions can be drawn about their ability to prevent deaths or improve patient outcomes. A serious outbreak continues to challenge Congo The research developments come as the DRC continues to face a major public health emergency. According to WHO's epidemiological update published on 12 November, the DRC had recorded 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 confirmed deaths, based on data available as of 11 November. The reported case-fatality ratio was approximately 49 per cent, while 3,045 people had recovered. The outbreak has placed considerable pressure on healthcare services, particularly in affected communities where access to timely medical assistance can be difficult. In remarks delivered on 11 November, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus highlighted both progress and continuing challenges. Although some areas were showing encouraging signs of slower transmission, new hotspots were still emerging and the outbreak remained uncontrolled overall. He also highlighted insecurity and attacks on healthcare facilities and response workers as major obstacles to containing the disease. Why the research matters A scientific illustration of an Ebola virus particle. The Bundibugyo virus is a distinct species of Ebola virus for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved. This makes the ongoing research particularly important. Although Ervebo has been used in previous Ebola responses, WHO has emphasised that its protection against Bundibugyo virus in humans has not been established. Its evaluation in research protocols is therefore essential to determine whether it can provide meaningful protection. The new candidates could help address this gap, but clinical trials must establish their safety and effectiveness before they can be considered successful. WHO expects initial findings from the treatment trials in the coming months, while results from the Tumaini vaccine trial are expected in early 2027. Hope, but no confirmed breakthrough yet Healthcare workers receive an Ebola vaccine in Beni, North Kivu, during the outbreak response in October 2026. The progress in vaccine and treatment research represents an important step in the international effort to respond to the outbreak. However, experts continue to emphasise that research alone will not bring the epidemic under control. Early diagnosis, appropriate supportive care, contact tracing, infection prevention, safe and dignified burials, and cooperation with affected communities remain essential parts of the response. For communities affected by the outbreak, the trials offer the possibility of better protection and treatment in the future. Their ultimate significance, however, will depend on the scientific evidence they produce. For now, the developments represent cautious optimism rather than a confirmed medical breakthrough, as researchers continue working towards effective tools against one of the most challenging Ebola virus diseases. According to WHO's epidemiological update published on 12 November, the DRC had recorded 11,197 confirmed cases and 5,471 confirmed deaths, based on data available as of 11 November. The reported case-fatality ratio was approximately 49 per cent, while 3,045 people had recovered. The outbreak has placed considerable pressure on healthcare services, particularly in affected communities where access to timely medical assistance can be difficult. In remarks delivered on 11 November, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus highlighted both progress and continuing challenges. Although some areas were showing encouraging signs of slower transmission, new hotspots were still emerging and the outbreak remained uncontrolled overall. He also highlighted insecurity and attacks on healthcare facilities and response workers as major obstacles to containing the disease. Why the research matters A scientific illustration of an Ebola virus particle. The Bundibugyo virus is a distinct species of Ebola virus for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved. This makes the ongoing research particularly important. Although Ervebo has been used in previous Ebola responses, WHO has emphasised that its protection against Bundibugyo virus in humans has not been established. Its evaluation in research protocols is therefore essential to determine whether it can provide meaningful protection. The new candidates could help address this gap, but clinical trials must establish their safety and effectiveness before they can be considered successful. WHO expects initial findings from the treatment trials in the coming months, while results from the Tumaini vaccine trial are expected in early 2027. Hope, but no confirmed breakthrough yet Healthcare workers receive an Ebola vaccine in Beni, North Kivu, during the outbreak response in October 2026. The progress in vaccine and treatment research represents an important step in the international effort to respond to the outbreak. However, experts continue to emphasise that research alone will not bring the epidemic under control. Early diagnosis, appropriate supportive care, contact tracing, infection prevention, safe and dignified burials, and cooperation with affected communities remain essential parts of the response. For communities affected by the outbreak, the trials offer the possibility of better protection and treatment in the future. Their ultimate significance, however, will depend on the scientific evidence they produce. For now, the developments represent cautious optimism rather than a confirmed medical breakthrough, as researchers continue working towards effective tools against one of the most challenging Ebola virus diseases. news.content: Skip to main content ePaper Football Leagues 26/27 Search K24 Digital News Entertainment Lifestyle Sports Health & Fitness Ebola: 2 vaccines to join DRC’s Tumaini trial as Kenya eyes Ksh4B study Willow Health 15th November, 2026 04:51 PM Updated 15th November, 2026 08:33 PM A medical officer at the lab. PHOTO/WHO For almost six months, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has fought an Ebola outbreak with no approved vaccine for the virus driving it. Since the outbreak was declared on May 15, 2026, it has recorded more than 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths, making it the largest in the country’s history. That gap may now narrow as two vaccine candidates developed specifically to protect against the Bundibugyo species of Ebola are set to join the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial in the DRC. It will be the first time vaccines designed for Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak of the disease. The World Health Organization (WHO) announced the decision on November 4, 2026. Its independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization recommended the pair after reviewing available preclinical and early clinical evidence. The two are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. Both build on technology proven during Covid-19. ChAdOx1 uses a modified chimpanzee adenovirus, the platform behind Oxford’s Covid-19 vaccine, to deliver genetic instructions for a protein on the surface of Bundibugyo virus. mRNA-1469 carries similar instructions in messenger RNA packaged in tiny lipid particles. According to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, both produced encouraging results in animal studies, and early trials in the United Kingdom and Canada suggest they can safely stimulate immune responses in humans. Tumaini, which means hope in Kiswahili, began in Bunia, where the first participant received a vaccine dose on October 26, 2026 WHO informed the developers on November 2, 2026, and the candidates will enter the trial only after receiving the necessary national approvals. “The fact that these vaccines are ready to enter clinical trials is a testament to the power of science and partnership,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. He thanked the scientists, health workers and partners involved, and “above all the trial participants, whose involvement would generate evidence that could help save lives.” Tumaini, which means hope in Kiswahili, began in Bunia, Eastern DRC, where the first participant received a vaccine dose on October 26, 2026. The Phase 2/3 trial tests several vaccine candidates against Bundibugyo virus within a single research framework, measuring their safety, immunogenicity and efficacy. Ervebo was the first vaccine to enter the trial. It is already licensed to prevent Ebola virus disease caused by Zaire ebolavirus, but its effectiveness against Bundibugyo virus has yet to be established. ChAdOx1 and mRNA-1469, already identified in efforts to widen Tumaini’s range of candidates, will give researchers options built specifically against the Bundibugyo species. The trial relies on ring vaccination where instead of targeting a whole population, teams identify people who have been in contact with someone confirmed to have Bundibugyo Virus Disease (BVD), and who are therefore at high risk of infection, and enrol them in vaccination rings. WHO says four rings have been established, with several more being prepared. They include contacts of people who fell ill or died. The approach draws on the West African outbreak about a decade ago, when a landmark trial in Guinea established Ervebo’s efficacy against Zaire ebolavirus. That experience lets Tumaini to assess vaccines while the response is still underway, rather than waiting for the outbreak to end. The burial of an Ebola victim. PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/IFRC Gavi has separately pledged up to US$40 million (Ksh5.2 billion) for manufacturing readiness For affected communities, the research could eventually offer a new tool against a species that has challenged existing Ebola vaccine efforts. The candidates, however, remain under investigation. Their place in the trial is not proof that they work, nor that they are approved for public use. Even a successful vaccine will not help people already infected. The PARTNERS trial, launched in July 2026, is evaluating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral drug remdesivir or a combination of both can improve survival among people with confirmed BVD. It is expected to expand to include a further candidate, maftivimab. A complementary post-exposure prophylaxis study involving obeldevisir is also underway. Through its Research and Development Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme, WHO helps develop protocols, gives strategic and technical advice, coordinates partners and supports the studies within the outbreak response. The Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB), the DRC’s national public health and biomedical research institute, leads Tumaini. It is supported by the University of Antwerp in Belgium, WHO, Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières, the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Antwerp and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC). Investment from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), which Gavi says exceeds US$75 million (Ksh9.8 billion), enabled the candidates’ rapid development. Gavi has separately pledged up to US$40 million (Ksh5.2 billion) for manufacturing readiness, so successful vaccines can be produced at scale. IAVI has received US$36 million (Ksh4.7 billion) to begin a trial in Kenya in January 2027 Kenya, which contained an imported outbreak of BVD, plans to join the search. Facebook Twitter Print Email DR Congo Ebola outbreak: Unrest fuelled by armed groups holds back response By Daniel Johnson, Geneva 13 November 2026 Health The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread amid repeated and ongoing deadly attacks on civilians and frontline health workers by armed groups that are obstructing efforts to stop transmission, UN responders said on Friday. In an update, the UN Senior Ebola Response Coordinator, Julien Harneis, stressed that more people are being killed by Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters than by Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in recent days. And yet attacks on “tens of villages" across the south of Ituri and North Kivu provinces go "unnoticed", Mr. Harneis maintained. “People are scared, people are furious at the lack of action on this...following up contact tracing in areas where ADF operating is a very hazardous idea.” Up to 500 infections per week Echoing that message, the UN World Health Organization (WHO)’s Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu, Executive Director of WHO’s Health Emergencies Programme, said that despite much progress in containing transmission within eastern DRC, about 400 to 500 cases of infection are still being identified every week. Tweet URL This trend is linked to the emergence of cases in rural and hard-to-reach areas. In more positive developments, the WHO official noted that prevention efforts have led to “a significant reduction” in transmission in previous hotspots, in particular Bunia, Mongbwalu, Rampara and Nizi, all in Ituri province in eastern DRC. Nonetheless, the violent unrest across the vast area impacted by Ebola creates huge challenges for responders. “We’ve seen so many attacks on healthcare, attacks on communities as well, attacks on people providing care, and people losing their lives, nurses in burials,” Dr Ihekweazu explained. “So, we need to keep working with the community, and this is very important. And working with the specific groups instigating these attacks.” Disease threats in addition to attacks Communities are already facing outbreaks of diseases, malnutrition and displacement driven by decades of violent unrest fuelled by dozens of armed groups that remain active in the resource-rich region. Earlier this week, WHO condemned attacks against frontline healthcare workers and community awareness officers, including in Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu that killed 66 civilians including three health workers. Three health facilities were also looted. Two weeks ago, a nurse was also killed and another health worker badly injured when they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in Tshopo province. Tedros appeal Other attacks have included an arson attempt on a treatment centre and stones thrown at a vehicle used for conducting safe and dignified burials, an indication of the need to continue to build trust with extremely vulnerable communities. “We cannot focus only on Ebola. Some people in the affected communities have said told me personally that Ebola is a lesser evil compared to some of the other threats they face,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus stressed earlier this week. A massive humanitarian emergency The DRC Ebola outbreak was declared in May and has since become the country's largest yet as it continues to spread faster than any previous outbreak across the vast east and northeast provinces. To date, more than 11,000 cases have been confirmed and more than 5,000 people have died. In a related development, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that nearly 29 million people in the DRC face acute food insecurity, with most in the conflict and Ebola-affected eastern and northeastern provinces. That number is likely to continue to increase, said Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP Director of Food Security and Nutrition Analysis. Briefing journalists via video in Geneva, Mr. Bauer stressed that conflict is driving the hunger crisis, in addition to the Ebola outbreak. “What we need right now is access, and we need resources to avoid the situation becoming more difficult in the DRC,” he said. Hunger emergency Latest UN-backed food insecurity expert assessments indicate that between January and June 2027, 30.3 million people will be in crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse, with 4.2 million of this number experiencing “emergency levels” of hunger and the most acute needs in North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri provinces “driven by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement”. Mr. Bauer noted that Ebola is just one of many disease outbreaks in DRC, but that it is compounding the hunger crisis for communities already struggling to eat. “Families are being displaced, they’re being cut off from their farms, from their livelihoods,” he explained. “Food prices are rising, making affording a meal quite complicated for too many households.” Ebola Facebook Twitter Print Email Back to top

analysis.brief_en: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to spread, particularly in rural and hard-to-reach areas, as armed groups like the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) obstruct response efforts. The Bundibugyo virus is the specific strain involved, with the World Health Organization (WHO) reporting 400 to 500 new cases per week. Despite progress in containing transmission in previous hotspots, the outbreak remains a significant public health challenge. The situation is further complicated by violent unrest, attacks on healthcare workers and facilities, and a concurrent humanitarian crisis marked by acute food insecurity affecting nearly 29 million people. The WHO and UN responders are working to strengthen prevention efforts and build trust with communities, but the ongoing conflict and insecurity hinder these initiatives. The outbreak, declared in May 2026, has resulted in over 11,000 confirmed cases and more than 5,000 deaths, making it the largest yet in the DRC. The humanitarian emergency is exacerbated by persistent conflict and large-scale displacement, with food prices rising and families being cut off from their livelihoods. The WHO has condemned attacks on frontline workers and emphasized the need for continued access and resources to address the crisis.

news.content: CHAIRMAN: DR. KHALID BIN THANI AL THANI EDITOR-IN-CHIEF: PROF. KHALID MUBARAK AL-SHAFI News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook Qatar Health General Education Government Weather Transport Culture How To? World Gulf Middle East Asia Europe Africa Americas Business Qatar Business Middle East Business World Business Stock Market Energy Sports Qatar Sport Football Formula One NBA Cricket Tennis Rally Athletics Motosports Golf Horse Racing Olympics Padel Cuesports Views Editor-in-Chief Opinion Editorial Doha Today Community Campus Souq Life Style Technology Motoring Feature & more Wellness Food Travel Fashion Science & Environment Entertainment Cinema Music In Focus Qatar 2022 Doha Expo Asian Cup IAAF Doha2019 Ramadan Qatar National Day World Cup 2026 News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook World / Africa After surviving Ebola, DR Congo doctors renew vow to fight the disease Published: 17 Nov 2026 - 05:20 pm | Last Updated: 17 Nov 2026 - 05:31 pm File photo Follow usnews Copy A+ A- Xinhua BENI, DR Congo: After spending 24 days in isolation battling Ebola, Congolese doctor Kinzi Divin knows all too well the dangers of the disease he has been fighting on the front line. Having survived an infection that has already claimed the lives of several of his colleagues, the doctor has emerged from the ordeal with his determination intact. "We will continue. We will continue to fight this disease," Divin told Xinhua after being declared Ebola-free at an Ebola treatment center in Beni, a city in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). His recovery offers a rare moment of relief amid a devastating outbreak that has killed more than 5,500 people nationwide since May, while putting the doctors and nurses fighting to contain it at deadly risks. Six months after the DRC declared the outbreak in May, the country has recorded 11,376 confirmed Ebola cases, including 5,568 deaths, as of Nov. 14, according to the latest official figures. The epidemic, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, has spread to 68 health zones across eight provinces, becoming the world's second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. Divin recalled that his ordeal began with what seemed like an ordinary headache after a demanding day at work. "I contracted the disease while working. I was at work, and when I came back, I just felt a little strange," he said. "It started with headaches, and I thought it was normal given the pressure of work. But as time went by, I noticed that other symptoms were beginning to appear." When diarrhea hit, Divin realized that the symptoms could indicate something far more serious than exhaustion. With his instinct as a medical professional, he decided to seek isolation immediately. He spent 24 days at the treatment center before finally recovering. However, surviving Ebola has not erased the emotional toll of watching fellow health workers succumb to the same virus. "We have seen what happened to two of our colleagues who lost their lives. It was really stressful. This is something that must not be taken lightly," he said. "We are on the front line, and that exposes us to great risks," Divin said. In Mabalako, another Ebola-affected health zone in North Kivu Province, nurse Muhindo Mbafumoja Shukuru experienced a similar experience. Shukuru said he contracted the virus through direct contact with patients under his care. "As nurses, we are really in direct contact with patients, and it was through this contact that I became infected," he recalled. He initially experienced headaches, chills and fever. A blood test subsequently confirmed that he had contracted Ebola. While grateful to have survived, he remains deeply troubled by the virus's continued spread. "The resurgence of this disease is really something that makes no one happy," he said. The experiences of Divin and Shukuru underscore the dangers confronting medical personnel in North Kivu, one of the hardest-hit provinces in the current Ebola outbreak. According to Guy Mutombo, head of operations for the Ebola response in North Kivu, over 150 frontline health workers have contracted the virus in the province, including nine doctors, four of whom have died. Beyond the human toll, Mutombo said shortages of essential medical supplies, particularly personal protective equipment (PPE), remain a major obstacle to protecting frontline personnel. "We face many difficulties, and the first is related to supplies, particularly what we call PPE," he said. The challenge comes as North Kivu continues to report new Ebola infections and deaths, putting additional pressure on an already strained health system. According to the latest situation report released by the DRC's health authorities, North Kivu had recorded 2,860 confirmed infections and 1,590 deaths as of Nov. 14, representing a case fatality rate of 55.6 percent, higher than the national average of 48.9 percent. Six months after the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak on May 15, the virus continues to spread across the country, testing the resilience of health workers and the capacity of the national response. Divin, who has experienced Ebola both as a doctor and as a patient, knows that the risks facing his colleagues remain far from over. Yet neither the days spent in isolation nor the deaths of fellow doctors have persuaded him to abandon the fight. "We will continue to fight this disease," he said. analysis.brief_en: In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), an ongoing Ebola outbreak has claimed over 5,500 lives since May 2026, with North Kivu Province being one of the hardest-hit areas. Kinzi Divin, a doctor who survived Ebola after 24 days of isolation, and nurse Muhindo Mbafumoja Shukuru, who contracted the virus through direct patient contact, highlight the risks faced by frontline workers. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, has resulted in 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths as of November 14, 2026, with a case fatality rate of 55.6% in North Kivu. Despite the personal toll, including the deaths of four doctors, Divin and others remain committed to combating the disease. The DRC's health authorities continue to monitor the situation, emphasizing the need for improved personal protective equipment (PPE) and containment efforts. The outbreak remains a significant public health challenge, with the health system under immense pressure.

analysis_en.time: Publication date: 2026-11-17. Event date: 24 days of isolation for Kinzi Divin. The outbreak began in May 2026 and continued into November 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically North Kivu Province and Beni city. Affected population includes healthcare workers, particularly doctors and nurses, and the general population in the eight provinces impacted by the outbreak.
analysis_en.event: Ebola virus outbreak in the DRC, with healthcare workers like Kinzi Divin and Muhindo Mbafumoja Shukuru contracting the virus while treating patients. The outbreak has resulted in confirmed cases and deaths, with the Bundibugyo Ebola virus identified as the causative agent.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: As of November 14, 2026, the DRC has recorded 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths. North Kivu Province alone has 2,860 confirmed infections and 1,590 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 55.6%. The outbreak has caused significant strain on the health system and exposed frontline workers to high risks.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The outbreak is ongoing, with healthcare workers continuing to fight the disease despite personal risks. The DRC's health authorities are releasing situation reports, and the response includes isolation, treatment, and efforts to address shortages of personal protective equipment (PPE). The situation remains under investigation and requires further containment measures.

news.title_zh: 在埃博拉病毒中幸存后,刚果民主共和国医生重申抗击这种疾病的誓言
news.source_body_en: In the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), an ongoing Ebola outbreak has claimed over 5,500 lives since May 2026, with North Kivu Province being one of the hardest-hit areas. Kinzi Divin, a doctor who survived Ebola after 24 days of isolation, and nurse Muhindo Mbafumoja Shukuru, who contracted the virus through direct patient contact, highlight the risks faced by frontline workers. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo Ebola virus, has resulted in 11,376 confirmed cases and 5,568 deaths as of November 14, 2026, with a case fatality rate of 55.6% in North Kivu. Despite the personal toll, including the deaths of four doctors, Divin and others remain committed to combating the disease. The DRC's health authorities continue to monitor the situation, emphasizing the need for improved personal protective equipment (PPE) and containment efforts. The outbreak remains a significant public health challenge, with the health system under immense pressure.

See latest updates Ebola outbreak in DR Congo remains out of control, six months into the response MSF teams are witnessing critical gaps as the response fails to reach communities. November 12, 2026 Share Share in FacebookShare in BlueSkyShare in LinkedInShare in TwitterShare in Mail Health care workers check each other's personal protective equipment to ensure proper fit before entering a high-risk area at an Ebola treatment center in North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF Related Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola Outbreaks and epidemics View more Related Democratic Republic of Congo Ebola Outbreaks and epidemics View more The second-largest Ebola disease outbreak in history remains out of control, six months after it was declared in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns. Despite the considerable resources mobilized for the response, too little is reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities. Urgent action is needed to ensure those resources translate into effective, coordinated activities where they are needed most. Victoire, a patient with Ebola disease, visits with his wife Kasoki at the Ebola Treatment Center in Kitatumba, in Butembo, North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF Critical supplies and support are not reaching areas that need them Hundreds of millions of dollars have been disbursed by the international community, yet critical shortcomings in essential aspects of the response persist, undermining efforts to halt the outbreak and save lives. “Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to stop the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets,” says Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF International President. “Our teams are often left speechless by the dysfunction they witness in many areas. Six months into the response, this situation is simply unacceptable.” These dysfunctions take many forms: untrained and unpaid response personnel, some of whom have gone on strike; vehicles and ambulances without fuel; surveillance teams that exist on paper but are nowhere to be seen on the ground; community workers without phones or mobile data to share alerts; and health care staff left without the supplies or technical support needed to handle suspected cases. A health care worker decontaminates a colleague's PPE at an Ebola treatment center in North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF Surveillance infrastructure is woefully lacking One of our greatest concerns is the persistent failure of the epidemiological surveillance system, a cornerstone of any Ebola response. Despite the resources officially allocated to this critical activity, surveillance remains deeply problematic, with entire areas poorly covered or even completely neglected. Over the past month, close to two-thirds of reported Ebola-related deaths have occurred in communities. “Data collected by MSF illustrates just how serious the problem is,” says Abdelmoneim. “Since the beginning of the response, in Ituri province, only 9 percent of patients with Ebola disease treated by our teams had previously been identified as contacts by the surveillance system. Although community mistrust makes surveillance difficult, urgent improvements in oversight, staffing, and operational support are essential.” A health care worker supervises infection prevention and control procedures at an Ebola treatment center in North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF Key areas are being overlooked amid the response MSF is also concerned about the excessive concentration of efforts in certain areas, at the expense of other hotspots where needs are increasingly urgent. For example, in North Kivu province, the response has been too slow to match the scale of the epidemic, while Haut-Uélé province remains dramatically overlooked. In both provinces, MSF has observed teams that are inadequately resourced to respond effectively, as well as health facilities operating without adequate sterilization capacity, water, chlorine, or triage systems. This has turned some facilities into new centers of transmission, rather than places of care that contribute to stopping the outbreak. In the Beni health zone, North Kivu province, close to three-quarters of Ebola patients contracted the disease in a health facility. Six months into the response, MSF continues to receive requests for personal protective equipment (PPE) from health facilities and humanitarian organizations, many of which we cannot fulfil. This is not just a question of operational effectiveness — it is also a question of restoring trust among communities that have already paid an enormous price. Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF International President “Too few responders are operating beyond the initial hotspot to tackle the spread of the virus in other hard-hit parts of the country,” says Abdelmoneim. “Meanwhile, private health providers, such as clinics, hospitals, and pharmacies, as well as traditional healers, remain largely forgotten from the response plans. Yet they are often first point of contact for people seeking care — and too often where they get infected. The response must be adapted to this reality. Otherwise, we risk spending years constantly playing catch-up with this outbreak.” Over the past six months, the Congolese authorities and their international partners have achieved tangible results: Diagnostic capacity has been strengthened; isolation and treatment units have expanded; community engagement activities have increased; and trials have been launched to identify treatments and develop vaccines. Despite the vast amounts of money provided for the response, many frontline responders are left trying to stop the outbreak with empty hands and empty pockets. Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF International President Yet the shortcomings of the Ebola response remain profound and largely unaddressed, despite being widely acknowledged. The Congolese authorities have announced measures aimed at strengthening oversight and transparency in the activities carried out by the different stakeholders involved in the response in order to provide a clearer understanding of how resources are being allocated and used. Commitments and announcements must now translate into concrete change on the ground. With the outbreak surpassing 11,000 cases and over 5,000 deaths, the need for action is urgent. The Congolese government and United Nations agencies must ensure that the resources already mobilized translate into an effective response. This means strengthening oversight and accountability, ensuring that response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards the areas where needs are greatest. “This is not just a question of operational effectiveness — it is also a question of restoring trust among communities that have already paid an enormous price,” says Abdelmoneim. Entrance of the Ebola Treatment Center in Kitatumba, Butembo, North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF How MSF is responding to the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo MSF was among the first organizations to support the Congolese authorities following the declaration of the outbreak on May 15, 2026. Over the past six months, MSF teams have been involved in setting up treatment centers and isolation facilities, strengthening infection prevention and control in health care facilities, conducting surveillance and community awareness activities, and sending rapid response teams to reach newly identified hotspots. As of early November, MSF's response covered five of the eight affected provinces. Teams continue to operate eight Ebola treatment centers, with three rapid response teams available. Over the past six months, approximately 1,500 patients with confirmed Ebola infections have been admitted to MSF-supported facilities. MSF has allocated more than $70 million to our Ebola response, funded almost entirely through private donations. Nearly 2,900 people, both working directly for or financially supported by MSF, are involved in these activities, approximately 90 percent of whom are locally recruited. Dr. Javid Abdelmoneim, MSF International President Yet the shortcomings of the Ebola response remain profound and largely unaddressed, despite being widely acknowledged. The Congolese authorities have announced measures aimed at strengthening oversight and transparency in the activities carried out by the different stakeholders involved in the response in order to provide a clearer understanding of how resources are being allocated and used. Commitments and announcements must now translate into concrete change on the ground. With the outbreak surpassing 11,000 cases and over 5,000 deaths, the need for action is urgent. The Congolese government and United Nations agencies must ensure that the resources already mobilized translate into an effective response. This means strengthening oversight and accountability, ensuring that response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards the areas where needs are greatest. “This is not just a question of operational effectiveness — it is also a question of restoring trust among communities that have already paid an enormous price,” says Abdelmoneim. Entrance of the Ebola Treatment Center in Kitatumba, Butembo, North Kivu province. | DR Congo 2026 © Elio Parfait/MSF How MSF is responding to the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo MSF was among the first organizations to support the Congolese authorities following the declaration of the outbreak on May 15, 2026. Over the past six months, MSF teams have been involved in setting up treatment centers and isolation facilities, strengthening infection prevention and control in health care facilities, conducting surveillance and community awareness activities, and sending rapid response teams to reach newly identified hotspots. As of early November, MSF's response covered five of the eight affected provinces. Teams continue to operate eight Ebola treatment centers, with three rapid response teams available. Over the past six months, approximately 1,500 patients with confirmed Ebola infections have been admitted to MSF-supported facilities. MSF has allocated more than $70 million to our Ebola response, funded almost entirely through private donations. Nearly 2,900 people, both working directly for or financially supported by MSF, are involved in these activities, approximately 90 percent of whom are locally recruited. Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|November 15, 2026 Ebola Outbreak Reaches 11,145 Cases, 5437 Deaths Advertisement The Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has reached 11,145 confirmed cases and 5437 confirmed deaths as of November 10, 2026, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).1 DRC accounts for 11,114 of those cases and 5433 deaths. The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record and is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks, CDC reports.1 Outside DRC, Kenya has reported 9 confirmed cases and 2 deaths, Uganda 20 confirmed cases and 2 deaths plus 1 probable case and 1 probable death, and Nigeria and France 1 confirmed case each.1 No cases tied to this outbreak have been reported in the US, and CDC considers the overall risk to the American public and travelers low.1 Confirmed deaths represent about 49% of confirmed cases. Investigation of additional cases is ongoing, and suspected cases and deaths in DRC are temporarily excluded from the count pending data standardization, so totals are expected to change.1 How Fast Is the 2026 Ebola Outbreak Spreading? The outbreak surpassed 1000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation.1 By comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1000 cases. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC.1 Cases have been confirmed in the DRC provinces of Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), Nord-Ubangi (North Ubangi), and Tshopo.1 South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Frequently Asked Questions What is Bundibugyo virus? Bundibugyo virus is a type of Ebola virus and the cause of the 2026 outbreak in DRC. CDC reports it is the virus driving cases in DRC, Kenya, and Nigeria. Have any Ebola cases been reported in the US during this outbreak? No. As of November 13, 2026, CDC reports no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak in the US and considers the risk to the American public low. What travel restrictions are in place? Travelers who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. Travelers from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. Ebola Cases Reported Outside DRC As of October 23, Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed 9 cases of Ebola disease and 2 deaths.1 The initial case, reported October 6, involved a man who traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he was hospitalized and died in an isolation unit. Subsequent cases, including the second death, occurred among relatives and health care providers in close contact with him, all of whom were already in quarantine when diagnosed.1 Kenya's Ministry of Health has reported no community spread, and all cases were in Nairobi.1 On October 20, Nigeria reported its first case in the 2026 outbreak, with testing confirming Bundibugyo virus.1 Uganda reported cases at the same time DRC declared the outbreak, with 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths overall.1 The last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026, and France's single patient was released on July 4.1 Neither country has reported active cases. US Travel Restrictions and CDC Response US entry for travelers recently in DRC remains temporarily restricted.1 Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. US citizens and nationals who have been in Uganda or South Sudan, but not DRC, within 21 days of arrival must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening.1 Since 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time on November 3, all passengers boarding an international flight to the US must attest they have not been in DRC during the 21 days before departure.1 CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Approximately 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries.1 Response Challenges for Clinicians and Public Health CDC cites limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, and frequent cross-border population movement as barriers to containment.1 Violence against health care workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to infections among health care workers treating patients. Mistrust of government and misinformation further complicate outreach.1 For US clinicians, CDC directs providers to its clinical guidance for Ebola disease, screening and diagnosis resources for viral hemorrhagic fevers, and infection prevention and control recommendations for US hospitals.1 A travel history covering the prior 21 days remains central to identifying patients at risk. Investigation of additional cases is ongoing, and suspected cases and deaths in DRC are temporarily excluded from the count pending data standardization, so totals are expected to change.1 How Fast Is the 2026 Ebola Outbreak Spreading? The outbreak surpassed 1000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation.1 By comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1000 cases. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC.1 Cases have been confirmed in the DRC provinces of Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), Nord-Ubangi (North Ubangi), and Tshopo.1 South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Frequently Asked Questions What is Bundibugyo virus? Bundibugyo virus is a type of Ebola virus and the cause of the 2026 outbreak in DRC. CDC reports it is the virus driving cases in DRC, Kenya, and Nigeria. Have any Ebola cases been reported in the US during this outbreak? No. As of November 13, 2026, CDC reports no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak in the US and considers the risk to the American public low. What travel restrictions are in place? Travelers who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. Travelers from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. Ebola Cases Reported Outside DRC As of October 23, Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed 9 cases of Ebola disease and 2 deaths.1 The initial case, reported October 6, involved a man who traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he was hospitalized and died in an isolation unit. Subsequent cases, including the second death, occurred among relatives and health care providers in close contact with him, all of whom were already in quarantine when diagnosed.1 Kenya's Ministry of Health has reported no community spread, and all cases were in Nairobi.1 On October 20, Nigeria reported its first case in the 2026 outbreak, with testing confirming Bundibugyo virus.1 Uganda reported cases at the same time DRC declared the outbreak, with 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths overall.1 The last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026, and France's single patient was released on July 4.1 Neither country has reported active cases. US Travel Restrictions and CDC Response US entry for travelers recently in DRC remains temporarily restricted.1 Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the US. US citizens and nationals who have been in Uganda or South Sudan, but not DRC, within 21 days of arrival must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening.1 Since 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time on November 3, all passengers boarding an international flight to the US must attest they have not been in DRC during the 21 days before departure.1 CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Approximately 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries.1 Response Challenges for Clinicians and Public Health CDC cites limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, and frequent cross-border population movement as barriers to containment.1 Violence against health care workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to infections among health care workers treating patients. Mistrust of government and misinformation further complicate outreach.1 For US clinicians, CDC directs providers to its clinical guidance for Ebola disease, screening and diagnosis resources for viral hemorrhagic fevers, and infection prevention and control recommendations for US hospitals.1 A travel history covering the prior 21 days remains central to identifying patients at risk. news.content_zh: 据美国疾病控制和预防中心 (CDC) 数据,截至 2026 年 11 月 10 日,刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 埃博拉疫情确诊病例已达 11,145 例,死亡病例达 5437 例。这是有记录以来第二大 暴发,确诊病例在刚果民主共和国的下韦莱省、上韦莱省、伊图里省、北基伍省、南基伍省、南乌班吉省、北乌班吉省和乔波省。在刚果民主共和国以外,肯尼亚报告了 9 例病例和 2 例死亡,乌干达有 20 例确诊病例和 2 例死亡,加上 1 例可能病例和 1 例可能死亡,尼日利亚和法国各有 1 例确诊病例。疾病预防控制中心表示,美国公众和旅行者面临的风险较低,美国尚未报告病例。暴发 的传播速度比以前更快,CDC 积极参与应对工作,拥有 500 多名工作人员,其中有 120 多名部署到受影响国家。对其他病例的调查正在进行中,疑似病例暂时排除在计数之外,等待数据标准化。疾病预防控制中心还建议避免前往刚果民主共和国的某些省份旅行以降低风险。
